Article Title: After a terrifying plane scare, Ted Leonsis wrote down 101 life goals, including owning a sports team; he bought the Washington Capitals for $85 million in 1999, and the franchise is now valued at $2.
Article Text:
Image: Sportico/ Getty Images

The plane scare that put owning a sports team on Ted Leonsis's bucket list

How Leonsis acquired the Washington Capitals for $85 million

Alex Ovechkin and the Capitals' first Stanley Cup

From a hockey franchise to a wider sports empire

Washington Capitals now valued at $2.55 billion

Leonsis's efforts to grow hockey beyond the Capitals

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A terrifying experience aboard a plane in 1983 prompted businessman Ted Leonsis to rethink how he wanted to live his life. After the aircraft experienced problems with its wing flaps and landing gear, he made a promise to himself to make the most of his time. He subsequently wrote down 101 things he wanted to achieve before dying, including owning a professional sports team and winning a championship. Years later, that ambition brought him to the Washington Capitals. Leonsis bought the NHL franchise in 1999 for $85 million as part of a broader deal involving other Washington sports interests. Forbes valued the Capitals at $2.55 billion in December 2025, making them the league's ninth-most valuable team.In 1983, Leonsis was aboard a plane that lost the ability to use its wing flaps and landing gear. The frightening incident made him reconsider his priorities. He later recalled deciding that if he survived, he would approach life differently.He began compiling a list of 101 things he wanted to do before he died. Among the ambitions were owning a professional sports team and winning a championship.The list eventually caught the attention of Dick Patrick, then president of the Washington Capitals.Patrick read about Leonsis's ambitions and recognised that he was not only a wealthy businessman but also a passionate hockey fan who regularly attended Capitals games.When Patrick approached him with the opportunity to buy the franchise, Leonsis initially hesitated. He was busy with his work at America Online (AOL) and was unsure whether he wanted to take on another major responsibility.However, after discussing the proposal with his wife, Lynn, he reconsidered. Leonsis recalled that she asked how he would feel if he accomplished 99 of his 101 goals but never bought the Washington team. Her question helped persuade him to go ahead with the purchase.In May 1999, Abe Pollin agreed to sell the Washington Capitals to an investment group led by Leonsis. The deal was valued at approximately $200 million, of which $85 million was allocated to the NHL franchise.The remaining $115 million covered minority interests in Washington Sports & Entertainment, which included the Washington Wizards and the MCI Center, now known as Capital One Arena, along with the right of first refusal to acquire the remaining holdings.Leonsis initially became the majority owner of the Capitals, with business partners Jonathan Ledecky and Dick Patrick holding minority stakes. The acquisition marked his entry into professional sports ownership and laid the foundation for his wider involvement in Washington's sports industry.One of the most significant developments in the franchise's history came in 2004, when Washington selected Russian forward Alex Ovechkin as the first overall pick in the NHL Draft.Ovechkin went on to become the team's captain and one of the most recognisable players in professional hockey. His arrival helped transform the Capitals into a consistent championship contender.The team's defining achievement came in 2018, when Washington defeated the Vegas Golden Knights in the Stanley Cup Final to win the first championship in franchise history. Ovechkin received the Conn Smythe Trophy as the most valuable player of the playoffs.The victory also fulfilled another ambition on Leonsis's 101-goal list: winning a championship. He later described the achievement as an important milestone in his journey as the team's owner.Leonsis's involvement in Washington sports expanded beyond the Capitals. In 2010, he and his partners completed the acquisition of the Washington Wizards, the arena and related sports businesses following the death of Abe Pollin.These assets became part of Monumental Sports & Entertainment, the company founded by Leonsis. Its portfolio includes the Capitals, the NBA's Washington Wizards, the WNBA's Washington Mystics, the Capital City Go-Go and other sports and entertainment operations.Capital One Arena, which opened in 1997 as the MCI Center, serves as a major venue for sporting events, concerts and other entertainment. The organisation has also invested in a substantial renovation of the arena, with Forbes reporting a three-year project worth approximately $800 million.The broader business brings together professional teams, venue operations, sponsorships, media and live entertainment, allowing the organisation to operate across several parts of the sports industry.The financial growth of the franchise has been substantial since Leonsis's investment in 1999. Forbes valued the Washington Capitals at $2.55 billion in December 2025, ranking them ninth among NHL teams.For the 2024-25 season, Forbes reported revenue of $282 million and $92 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA). The franchise also recorded $110 million in gate receipts, including club seats.The $2.55 billion figure is an estimated franchise valuation, rather than a confirmed sale price or Leonsis's personal profit from the investment. It reflects the team's commercial value, its position in the Washington market and the wider economics of professional hockey.Alongside the team's commercial and sporting growth, Leonsis has backed initiatives aimed at making hockey more accessible in the Washington region.The Capitals' Future Caps Learn to Play programme, launched in 2016, has introduced more than 12,000 participants to the sport. The organisation has also reported more than 30,000 participants in youth hockey events since 2018 and the construction or refurbishment of 14 outdoor street and inline hockey rinks.According to the NHL, registered youth and adult hockey participation in Washington, DC, increased by more than 220% between the 2005-06 and 2025-26 seasons. The number of registered girls and women players across Washington, Maryland and Virginia also rose by 225% during that period.Leonsis, who became chairman of the NHL's Board of Governors, was selected to receive the 2026 Lester Patrick Trophy for outstanding service to hockey in the United States. The recognition reflects his involvement in the sport beyond the performance of the Capitals.What began as a list of 101 ambitions after a frightening flight eventually led Leonsis to one of the most valuable franchises in professional hockey. His purchase fulfilled two of those goals: owning a sports team and winning a championship.
Article Summary: Ted Leonsis wrote a list of 101 things he wanted to do before he died. Among the ambitions were owning a professional sports team and winning a championship. He bought the Washington Capitals for $85 million in 1999. Forbes valued the Capitals at $2.55 billion in December 2025.

Article Title: An Australian former teacher began tanning animal hides and turned skins from invasive foxes and deer into clothing; her sideline has become a full-time business, even as scientists question its impac
Article Text:
Demand for ethically sourced fur and handcrafted products is growing

How a teacher built a fur business

Young consumers show interest in fur

Taxidermy and handmade products gain attention

Experts warn against relying on the fur trade

Hunters and leather workers find use for hides

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A former teacher in Australia has turned her interest in tanning animal hides into a full-time business, making clothing and accessories from invasive animals such as foxes and deer. ABC news reported about the business that works with hunters and supplies products to consumers interested in ethically sourced fur.Her creations have also attracted younger consumers. One of them, 22-year-old Amity Scarth, wears a rabbit-fur vest and a fox-fur scarf. She told ABC that she prefers fur made from animals considered pests in Australia rather than products sourced from fur farms.However, the growing interest in feral animal products has raised questions about whether the trade can help control invasive species. Experts warn that while using the hides of animals already killed can prevent waste, businesses dependent on a regular supply of these animals could eventually conflict with pest-control efforts.Heidi Beynon, a former art and woodwork teacher, did not initially plan to enter the fur industry. Her interest developed through goat farming, when she decided to tan the hides of goats harvested for meat. "I absolutely love goats and I sell goats mainly alive," she told ABC."But then we harvested some for meat and so I tanned the hides," she added.She later connected with hunters who dealt with feral deer and foxes. This gave her access to more animal hides, which she began turning into clothing and other products.The work eventually became her full-time occupation. She has also hired someone part-time to help manage the demand.Beynon says her approach makes use of animals that would otherwise be discarded after being culled. "People appreciate what I'm doing, and they see it as a valuable, beautiful, authentic product," she said. "I'm using something that would otherwise be wasted because they're going to be culled anyway."Scarth is among those who have embraced the products. She says she chooses fur based on its source and insists that the animals must be invasive species, killed ethically, with their hides processed and made into clothing in Australia.She also believes natural fur can last longer than many mass-produced fashion products. "Fur is designed to last a really long time," she said to ABC.She argues that natural fur has an environmental advantage over some synthetic materials because it can biodegrade if discarded.Scarth also rejects fur obtained from farms where animals are raised for their skins. "Fur that's not coming from sustainable sources is coming from fur farms, which are obviously extremely cruel."She hopes more consumers will become interested in reusing animal fur rather than relying on conventional fashion products.Interest in animal-based crafts is also visible at Australia's Oddities and Curiosities Expo, which features taxidermy, sustainable leather and handcrafted goods.Michelle Cozzaglio, one of the expo's founders, said the Australian event received around 2,000 applications this year. Its North American editions attracted about 4,000 applications.The exhibits include preserved animals, skulls, bones and unusual creations. Cozzaglio said humorous taxidermy, including preserved animals dressed in clothing, had also become popular. The expo offers taxidermy classes for people interested in learning the practice.Jack Gough from the Invasive Species Council said using feral animal products does not necessarily reduce their populations.He explained that deer numbers require sustained control measures to prevent population growth. "For deer, you need to remove about 35 to 50 per cent of the deer every year just to stop the population growing," he said.He warned that removing animals without exceeding their population growth rate would not reduce their numbers or density in an area.Gough also raised concerns about commercial industries that depend on a continuing supply of feral animals. Such businesses could eventually oppose measures aimed at reducing those populations.He said using animals for fur or meat could be ethical on a small scale, but larger industries might develop interests that work against effective pest control.Kurt Gale, who runs a vertebrate pest management organisation on the New South Wales Mid North Coast, primarily targets feral deer. The animals compete with livestock for food on grazing properties, and he sometimes removes as many as 30 deer from a property.Gale said using their meat, hides and skulls was preferable to leaving the remains unused. "If we can't use them, they get wasted in the paddock, so having them used in any way they can, whether that's meat or the hides or the skulls, then that's a great outcome," he said.He has partnered with leather worker Charlie Ginty, who conducts hide-tanning workshops. Participants range from 18-year-olds to people in their 60s.Ginty wants the workshops to teach both the tanning process and the importance of understanding the wider industry.For Scarth, turning invasive animal fur into clothing offers a way to combine fashion with the reuse of materials. She hopes the approach will become more popular."I think it's a really beautiful thing that we can re-purpose pest fur and turn that into something slow fashion, something beautiful, something ethical," she said.However, experts maintain that making use of feral animal hides is not the same as controlling their populations. A commercial market may reduce waste, but it cannot replace sustained pest-management efforts.
Article Summary: A former teacher in Australia has turned her interest in tanning animal hides into a full-time business. She makes clothing and accessories from invasive animals such as foxes and deer. Experts warn that businesses dependent on a regular supply of these animals could eventually conflict with pest-control efforts.

Article Title: California student Aanya Pradip creates ‘Giving Tree Produce’, a nonprofit platform connecting surplus backyard fruit with people in need
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

How a hackathon idea became a nonprofit to reduce food waste

PC: Giving Tree Produce

‘Giving Tree Produce’ creates a marketplace for surplus fruits and vegetables

How does ‘Giving Tree Produce’ plan to get surplus food to people in need

‘Giving Tree Produce’ team hopes to reach more Milpitas residents

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A student from Milpitas, California, has started a nonprofit to stop surplus backyard fruit from going to waste. Aanya Pradip founded ‘Giving Tree Produce’ after noticing that many families had more fruit growing in their gardens than they could use. She teamed up with a friend to build a website during a hackathon. The platform allows residents to list their extra fruits and vegetables so others can claim them for free.According to The Milpitas Beat, the project aims to connect people with surplus produce to those who need it. It also plans to donate fruits and vegetables to local food pantries. Pradip and a team of student volunteers have soft-launched the initiative and are working to reach more residents in Milpitas.Pradip first developed the idea at Los Altos Hacks during the hackathon she took part in. She and a friend created a website intended to reduce the amount of fruit and vegetables wasted in the community. The project grew from something she had noticed in her neighbourhood, that is trees in neighbourhood gardens and backyards were full of fruit that families could not eat.The website was designed to help residents share their surplus produce with others instead of letting it go to waste.After the hackathon, Pradip continued developing the idea and established ‘Giving Tree Produce’ as a nonprofit organisation to collect extra backyard fruits and vegetables and make them available to people who need them.‘Giving Tree Produce’ has a website and an app through which residents can offer fruit and vegetables they do not need. Donors list their surplus on the platform, where it appears on a page called Marketplace. People can then browse the listings and claim the produce they want. Pradip said collection can be arranged in different ways.A recipient may visit the donor’s home, ask one of the organisation’s volunteers to deliver the items, or arrange to meet the donor at a public location. The produce is free for everyone who claims it. This gives residents a way to share what is growing in their backyards instead of allowing usable food to go to waste.The organisation’s work is not limited to connecting individual residents with surplus produce. ‘Giving Tree Produce’ also aims to donate collected fruits and vegetables to local food pantries. Although the produce listed on the platform is free, people can make cash donations to the nonprofit. All proceeds from those donations will go to local food pantries.The project was started against a wider backdrop of food waste in the United States. The nonprofit is focused on addressing waste within the Milpitas community. By allowing residents to share extra backyard produce, it aims to make more fresh fruits and vegetables available to people who can use them.Pradip is working on the initiative with a team of between 5 and 10 volunteers, all of whom are students at Milpitas High School. The group has soft-launched ‘Giving Tree Produce’ and was hoping to hold its official launch in September or October as of August 2026.Pradip hopes more people in Milpitas will learn about the organisation and begin using it. She said, “Tech has the ability to give life to our ideas. And that’s why I really wanted to pursue this.” The students are also using Nextdoor to spread awareness and encourage more residents to list their surplus fruits and vegetables on the platform.
Article Summary: ‘Giving Tree Produce’ has a website and an app through which residents can offer fruit and vegetables they do not need. Donors list their surplus on the platform, where it appears on a page called Marketplace. People can then browse the listings and claim the produce they want. The produce is free for everyone who claims it.

Article Title: Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife MacKenzie Scott gives another $8 million to Atlanta students as her charitable donations cross $26 billion, yet her fortune remains above $27 billion with Amazon shares continuing
Article Text:
MacKenzie Scott's $8 million gift helps Atlanta students pursue college

What six-year graduation figures reveal about the scholarship programme

A separate $4.5 million contribution supports women returning to education

Why Scott's wealth has remained above $27 billion

MacKenzie Scott backs HBCUs and charities with billions in donations

MacKenzie Scott looks beyond donations to support social impact businesses

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

MacKenzie Scott has continued directing large sums towards education and community organisations, even as her personal fortune remains among the largest in the world. As reported, her latest contribution is an $8 million donation to Achieve Atlanta, a nonprofit supporting students from Atlanta's public schools with the cost of higher education. It is the second time Scott has made a gift of the same size to the organisation, taking her contributions to $16 million. The donation comes as the philanthropist's cumulative charitable giving has crossed $26 billion. Yet, despite the scale of those contributions, her wealth is still estimated to exceed $27 billion, helped in part by the performance of Amazon shares.Achieve Atlanta confirmed the latest contribution last week, four years after Scott first donated $8 million to the organisation. Its work centres on helping graduates of Atlanta Public Schools move into higher education, with financial assistance and guidance extending beyond the initial college application.The scholarship programme provides different levels of support depending on the type of institution students attend. Those pursuing a four-year bachelor's degree can receive need-based assistance of up to $20,000 across four years.Students enrolled in two-year colleges or technical programmes are eligible for annual awards of $1,500, available for as many as four semesters.Students also receive help with identifying suitable colleges, completing applications and preparing for employment after graduation. Achieve Atlanta Scholars confirmed its establishment in 2015, and has distributed more than $75 million in scholarships.The organisation's work has also been examined through an independent assessment involving researchers associated with Georgia State University's Georgia Policy Labs. The evaluation compared Achieve Atlanta scholarship recipients with other graduates of Atlanta Public Schools who had similar academic and demographic backgrounds but entered college without the programme's financial support.The findings showed a difference in how students progressed after enrolling. Fortune reported, around 91% of scholarship recipients returned for their second semester, against 77% of students in the comparison group. Six years after completing high school, 42% of the students who had received Achieve Atlanta support had graduated from college. The corresponding figure among comparable students without the programme's assistance was 36%.Achieve Atlanta referred to Scott's second contribution as recognition of its approach to supporting students beyond high school. The organisation said the continued funding would help sustain its postsecondary education work.Scott's latest charitable activity in Georgia has not been limited to young people entering college. Another education-focused organisation, the Jeannette Rankin Foundation, confirmed $4.5 million from the philanthropist. Based in Athens, Georgia, the foundation works with women aged 35 and older who want to pursue education but face financial barriers. The contribution is its largest single donation to date, according to The Atlanta Journal-Constitution.Foundation chief executive Karen Sterk told the newspaper that the funding could potentially benefit more than one million women. The organisation's work focuses on making educational opportunities accessible to women who may have had to put their studies aside because of financial circumstances or other responsibilities.Scott's charitable giving has reached a scale that would substantially reduce most personal fortunes. Her own financial position, however, has been shaped by the continued appreciation of the Amazon shares she received following her divorce from Jeff Bezos. The couple finalised their divorce in July 2019 after 25 years of marriage. Under the settlement, Scott received approximately 4% of Amazon, with the stake valued at around $37 billion at the time, as reported by Fortune.Since then, she has distributed more than $26 billion through over 2,700 donations to nonprofit organisations, according to Yield Giving, the philanthropic organisation she established. Forbes nevertheless estimates her current net worth at more than $27 billion.Her ownership of Amazon has reduced considerably. A regulatory filing showed that her holdings in the company fell by 42% during the year ending September 2025. The value of the shares she continues to hold has also changed the picture. Amazon's stock gained more than 42% over the five-year period ending in July 2026, according to figures previously reported by Fortune. The increase has helped offset the financial impact of her substantial charitable contributions.Amazon's position in the corporate world has also strengthened. The company secured the top position in the 2026 Fortune 500 ranking, becoming the largest US company by revenue and ending Walmart's 13-year run at the top of the list.Scott's education-related contributions have followed a pattern of supporting institutions and communities that often receive less attention from major donors. Her giving has included historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs), community colleges and tribal colleges, rather than being concentrated among the country's best-known private universities.Her donations to HBCUs alone have exceeded $1 billion, Fortune has reported. Other major contributions have reached organisations working in areas such as housing, children's welfare and reproductive healthcare. Among her largest reported gifts are $436 million to Habitat for Humanity, $281 million to Boys & Girls Clubs of America and $275 million to Planned Parenthood.Scott also joined the Giving Pledge in 2019, committing to give away most of her wealth during her lifetime or through her will. The initiative was established by philanthropists Warren Buffett and Bill and Melinda Gates to encourage wealthy individuals to dedicate the majority of their fortunes to charitable causes.Her philanthropic plans extend beyond transferring money directly to nonprofit organisations. In a 2024 Yield Giving essay, Scott discussed how she wanted her investment portfolio to support some of the same causes that guide her charitable contributions. She explained that she had asked her investment team to identify funds and businesses addressing social challenges, including affordable housing and digital healthcare services for women.The intention was to direct capital towards enterprises working in areas where she also wanted to make a difference through philanthropy.Scott also described a preference for investments in businesses led by people who understand the communities they serve. This includes founders from backgrounds that can make it harder to secure conventional funding, particularly women and people of colour.In her 2019 Giving Pledge letter, Scott had already outlined her intention to continue distributing her wealth rather than wait for a later stage of life. She wrote that the process would require time, effort and care, but that she would continue until her fortune had been given away.
Article Summary: MacKenzie Scott has donated $8 million to a scholarship programme in Atlanta, Georgia. A separate $4.5 million contribution supports women returning to education. The philanthropist's cumulative charitable giving has crossed $26 billion. Yet, despite the scale of those contributions, her wealth is still estimated to exceed $27 billion.

Article Title: Spain's Canary Islands see record single-day influx of migrants as nearly 2,000 reach archipelago
Article Text:
Migrants crowd a wooden boat as they arrive at the port of La Restinga on the Canary Island of El Hierro, Spain, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. (AP Photo)

A dangerous route, yet thousands continue to cross

Can migration issue influence Spain's election

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

(With AP inputs)

Nearly 2,000 migrants reached Spain's Canary Islands on Tuesday, setting a new record for the highest number of arrivals in the archipelago in a single day, Spanish authorities said.According to Spain's maritime rescue service, a total of 1,990 people arrived in 15 boats, with search and rescue vessels escorting the boats one after another to the small island of El Hierro."Sadly, this is a historic day," Canary Islands regional leader Fernando Clavijo told Spanish radio station Cadena SER.Clavijo added that around 100 minors were among those who arrived, including a four-day-old baby born during the journey.The previous single-day record was set just two weeks earlier, on November 7, when 1,400 people reached Gran Canaria, another island in the archipelago.The Canary Islands, located off the coast of West Africa, are a popular tourist destination for Europeans, thanks to their mild weather throughout the year. However, the archipelago has also become a key entry point for migrants seeking to reach Europe, despite the extremely dangerous journey that has claimed thousands of lives.The islands, located off the coast of West Africa, witnessed a surge in arrivals just ahead of Spain's national election later this week, with migration expected to be a major concern for many voters.Although the islands lie around 65 miles (105 kilometres) from the nearest African coast, many migrants take the route to evade security forces. The journeys can last several days or even weeks, with many boats missing their intended destination and drifting into the open Atlantic.More than 26,000 people have reached the Canary Islands this year, with nearly half of that number arriving in November alone.Departures from West Africa are seasonal, and November often sees a spike in numbers as many migrants attempt the crossing before the ocean becomes rough during winter. Relatively calm sea conditions in recent days have also contributed to the high number of departures.Most of the boats that arrived on Tuesday were carrying migrants from Senegal and Gambia. Despite the European Union's efforts to reduce migration from West Africa, many believe leaving their home countries is their only option to find work and build a better life.Spain's conservative Popular Party is seeking to unseat the ruling Socialist-led central government in Sunday's elections. For this, it would likely need to form a coalition with the far-right Vox party, which has made the expulsion of migrants and social policies favouring Spaniards over recent arrivals a key part of its campaign.Without directly naming Vox, Clavijo, the Canary Islands leader who belongs to the regional Canary Coalition party, condemned attempts to demonise migrants, describing them as "a xenophobic discourse of bad people".He also criticised a recent agreement by Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands to send migrants to Rwanda, calling it "ridiculous"."Europe is on the wrong path," Clavijo said.
Article Summary: Nearly 2,000 migrants reached Spain's Canary Islands on Tuesday, setting a new record for the highest number of arrivals in the archipelago in a single day. The islands, located off the coast of West Africa, witnessed a surge in arrivals just ahead of Spain's national election later this week.

Article Title: A historic British harbour clock house once placed on a heritage at-risk register has been restored through a £7.5 million project; its unusual local meridian runs five minutes and 41 seconds ahead of
Article Text:
Image Courtesy: Thanet District Council

A clock house with its own sense of time

From a heritage building at risk to a new harbour landmark

What will visitors find inside?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A new chapter for Ramsgate's Royal Harbour

Imagine arriving at a railway station in Ramsgate, checking the time on your watch and then discovering that the town's clocks are running almost 6 minutes ahead of the rest of the country. It might sound like a recipe for disaster, missed trains and confused travellers, but there was a time when this was perfectly normal. The coastal town in Kent once followed its own local time, known as Ramsgate Mean Time, calculated using a meridian that ran five minutes and 41 seconds ahead of Greenwich.Now, the historic building that housed this unusual piece of local history has a new lease on life. Ramsgate's Clock House, a Grade II* listed landmark on the town's Royal Harbour, has undergone a £7.5 million restoration after years of disrepair and being placed on Historic England's Heritage at Risk Register. The main construction work has now been completed, bringing the much-loved harbour building a step closer to welcoming visitors again.Built in 1817 and designed by architects Benjamin Wyatt and George Louch, the Clock House is one of the most recognisable historic buildings along Ramsgate's Royal Harbour. Its maritime connection goes beyond its location. The building once housed the Ramsgate Meridian, a brass line used to calculate the town's own local mean time.As explained by Visit Ramsgate , Ramsgate Mean Time was five minutes and 41 seconds ahead of Greenwich Mean Time. Before standardised time became widely adopted, towns and cities could follow their own local time, generally calculated according to the position of the sun. This meant that noon in one place did not necessarily correspond to noon somewhere else.Ramsgate's arrangement eventually became rather inconvenient. With regular trains arriving in the town, having a different local time could cause confusion for passengers trying to catch their connections or make their way to the harbour. The town eventually reverted to Greenwich Mean Time, but its unusual meridian remains an important part of its history.The restored Clock House will preserve that connection through a brass replica of the historic Ramsgate Meridian Line, allowing visitors to see a reminder of the time when the town quite literally ran on its own clock.For a building that has stood beside the harbour for more than two centuries, the Clock House had fallen into a rather unfortunate state. Years of deterioration left the historic structure in need of extensive repairs, eventually earning it a place on Historic England's Heritage at Risk Register.The restoration, delivered by Thanet District Council in partnership with construction company Willmott Dixon, has focused on preserving the building's historic character while making it suitable for modern public use. According to the council's announcement , the project involved an extensive overhaul of the structure, with particular care taken to protect its solid stone construction. Thanet District Council's £7.5 million investment is part of a wider regeneration effort aimed at bringing new life to Ramsgate's Royal Harbour. The council says the work has transformed the building into a heritage hub and community space for residents and visitors. In the announcement , Councillor Rick Everitt, Leader of Thanet District Council, described the project as a way of saving a piece of the town's maritime history and creating a new cultural centre for the harbour. Richard Poulter, Managing Director at Willmott Dixon Construction South, also highlighted the challenges involved in restoring a Grade II* listed building with significant structural and environmental issues.The restored Clock House is being adapted to offer more than a glimpse into its past. Plans include a flexible exhibition space celebrating Ramsgate's maritime history, alongside a new café extension with seating overlooking the harbour. The existing containers beside the building have also been removed as part of the wider project.The council's Clock House project page explains that the restoration and extension are intended to create a destination for both locals and visitors, rather than simply repair an old building. The museum experience is also being reimagined, with specialists working on how the town's history and collections can be presented through exhibitions.There is still some work to be done before the full experience is ready. While the main structural and building works have been completed, the internal exhibition fittings and community programming are continuing. The new café is expected to open in the coming months, with the restored spaces being prepared for public use.To celebrate the completion of the main construction works, Thanet District Council has announced a public drop-in event at the Clock House and Pier Yard on Wednesday, 25 November 2026. The event will include a ribbon-cutting ceremony and the inaugural chime of the restored clock mechanism, bringing its sound back across the harbour.For Ramsgate, the restoration is about more than giving an old clock house a fresh coat of life. It is an opportunity to reconnect with the town's maritime past, preserve an unusual piece of local history and give residents a space they can enjoy for years to come. And somewhere inside the restored building, the brass meridian will still tell its rather charming story of a town that once kept time a little differently.
Article Summary: Ramsgate's Clock House, a Grade II* listed landmark, has undergone a £7.5 million restoration. The building once housed the Ramsgate Meridian, a brass line used to calculate the town's own local mean time. Ramsgate Mean Time was calculated using a meridian that ran five minutes and 41 seconds ahead of Greenwich.

Article Title: A non-venomous snake that does not constrict its prey can still kill with its bite: a study of three Drymarchon species found their jaws generate tissue-damaging pressure greater than constriction by

Drymarchon

Drymarchon

What the researchers measured

Drymarchon

D. corais, D. couperi and D. melanurus

Drymarchon

A skull built to stretch

Drymarchon
