A way further

Wandering around the forests, you come across a snake. You would imagine that either the poison could kill you or the snake would squeeze you to death. You wouldn’t normally imagine that a bite by a non-venomous snake would kill you. Yet, a new study on three of thesnake species has found a new way a snake could kill.is a genus of large, nonvenomous, colubrid snakes commonly known as indigo snakes or cribos. These snakes are found in the Southeastern United States, Mexico, Central America, and South America. Their appetite consists of a wide variety of beings, from mammals, birds and amphibians to fish, eggs and other reptiles.The usual ways snakes subdue prey are described by researchers as envenomation or constriction; however, these large-bodied, non-venomous, non-constricting snakes often rely on simple seizing and pinioning techniques. While pinioning implies pinning prey against the ground or another surface, seizing involves grabbing it with the jaws.The study, " Beyond Venom and Constriction: Bite Performance and Trophic Ecology in the Genus Drymarchon " was published in the journal Zoology in September 2026. The team of researchers looked at three species of the genus. They measured the bodies and bite performance of 15 snakes and went through existing records of what the genus eats.The researchers observed that as expected, bigger heads gave stronger bites. However, bite force wasn’t correlated to body length because these snakes grow relatively longer while their heads grow proportionally smaller. This does have an effect on the strength of their jaws, though.Further, they compared bite pressure with constriction pressure in snakes of similar size. Thebites generated pressures capable of exceeding those produced by constricting snakes. In other words, the pressure concentrated between their jaws could be more damaging to prey tissue than the pressure applied by another snake wrapping its body around its victim.The researchers also identified prolonged jaw engagement and persistence as important parts of their hunting strategy. It is not simply about delivering one powerful bite and letting go. Holding on and continuing to apply pressure can make the attack lethal.Snakes have highly flexible skulls, an anatomical feature that allows them to swallow prey much wider than their own heads. Their jaws are not joined in the same rigid way as those of humans and many other animals. Instead, several movable bones work together, allowing the mouth to stretch around large meals.The flexibility, however, also leads to a less rigid skull structure. While taking a bite, a skull that moves easily will not provide the rigidity to apply high pressure. Thus, it was usually seen as a restriction to how much force snakes can apply, while flexibility was seen as necessary to swallow large prey.appears to challenge this expectation. Despite having the characteristic mobile skull of a snake, it has evolved an impressive ability to deliver concentrated biting pressure. Its feeding strategy demonstrates that flexibility and strength do not necessarily have to work against each other.Venom and constriction get most of the attention in snake research, and the indigo snake shows what that focus can miss. It has no venom and no coils. It grabs its prey, bites hard, and hangs on. The study measured bite pressure that exceeded constriction pressure in snakes of similar size, which suggests that simple seizing deserves the same scrutiny as the famous methods.Thus, researchers have brought light to new arenas of study in snake research that require greater attention.
Article Summary: The Eastern Indigo Snake has no venom and no coils. It grabs its prey, bites hard, and hangs on. The study measured bite pressure that exceeded constriction pressure in snakes of similar size. It suggests that simple seizing deserves the same scrutiny as the famous methods.

Article Title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan seeks execution delay, says he was defending Taliban
Article Text:
File photo: Nidal Hasan, charged with killing 13 people and wounding 31 in a November 2009 shooting spree at Fort Hood

Hasan wants to revive defence barred at trial

What happened in the Fort Hood attack?

Execution controversy and survivors’ objections

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan has asked a federal court to delay his scheduled execution, saying he intends to argue that he was defending the Taliban from an unlawful US military attack.In a court filing signed by Hasan on Tuesday, he said he intended to demonstrate that the military court’s judgment and his death sentence had been obtained and were being maintained in violation of his federal constitutional and statutory rights.The filing could delay the Trump administration’s plans to execute Hasan on December 3. A hearing has been scheduled for Wednesday morning.Hasan, who is representing himself with assistance from lawyers at the American Civil Liberties Union’s Capital Punishment Project, said he intended to continue representing himself in the legal fight.One of Hasan’s central arguments is that he was prevented from presenting a defence that his actions were legally justified because he was trying to protect the Afghan Taliban from what he described as an unlawful attack by the US Army.Hasan had argued that he was acting in “defense of others”, according to court documents. However, the military judge barred him from presenting that argument during his 2013 trial.After dismissing his lawyers and choosing to represent himself, Hasan largely remained silent during the three-week trial.While the military called nearly 90 witnesses, Hasan called none in his defence and made no closing argument.A military jury found him guilty of multiple counts of murder and attempted murder for the shooting, which left 13 people dead and 32 wounded.The case has been assigned to US district judge Tony Mattivi in Kansas, where Hasan is being held at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth. Mattivi was nominated by president Donald Trump and confirmed by the Senate in June.On November 5, 2009, Hasan walked into the Soldier Readiness Processing Center at Fort Hood, Texas, where soldiers were waiting for medical tests and preparing for deployment.He opened fire with a handgun fitted with laser sights, killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others.Hasan was shot by law enforcement officers during the attack, leaving him paralysed from the waist down and confined to a wheelchair.He was convicted by a military jury in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. The jury sentenced him to death.Trump authorised Hasan’s execution on the recommendation of defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The execution, scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, would be the first US military execution by firing squad since World War II and the first military execution since 1961.The plan drew controversy after Hegseth announced that the execution would be public and the Pentagon confirmed it would be livestreamed. Critics from both parties raised concerns that broadcasting the execution could fuel radicalisation and turn it into a spectacle.Trump later said the execution would not be livestreamed, but that immediate family members of the victims could witness it in person if they chose.The latest court filing comes amid further dispute over who will be allowed to attend. Military officials have denied requests from three survivors of the 2009 shooting to witness the execution, citing regulations, security and space constraints.The survivors argued that the military should recognise them as victims under a broader definition that includes direct physical, emotional or financial harm. The Army rejected their appeal, saying regulations specify who may attend a military execution.
Article Summary: Nidal Hasan killed 13 people and wounded 31 in a November 2009 shooting spree. He was convicted by a military jury in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder. The jury sentenced him to death and he was due to be executed on December 3. Hasan has asked a federal court to delay his scheduled execution. He intends to argue he was defending the Taliban from an unlawful US military attack.

Article Title: 2 children among 6 killed in plane crash off Mississippi coast in US
Article Text:
Cessna crashes off Mississippi coast (Representative image)

Six people, including two children, were found dead after a Cessna 210 aircraft crashed into the Gulf of Mexico off the Mississippi coast on Tuesday, news agency AP cited US Coast Guard.Divers recovered the bodies after the aircraft went down in the Gulf between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island, part of the Gulf Islands National Seashore.The plane was carrying four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros said.Rescue teams had spent several hours searching for the missing passengers. Initial search efforts led to the discovery of three life jackets, a life raft and the aircraft's cabin floating in the water, Ros said.According to flight-tracking website FlightAware, the Cessna was travelling from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, when it crashed.
Article Summary: Divers recovered the bodies after the aircraft went down in the Gulf. The plane was carrying four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10. The Cessna was travelling from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, when it crashed.

Article Title: ‘Justice is not for sale’: California governor Newsom demands federal reforms to limit presidential pardon powers
Article Text:
Newsom targets Trump over pardons, alleges clemency has become a business under his watch

Trump hits back at Newsom

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

California governor Gavin Newsom has called for sweeping federal reforms to the US president's power to grant pardons, accusing President Donald Trump of using the Justice Department to protect wealthy allies and politically connected individuals.He alleged that clemency had become a business under the Trump administration.In a post on X, Newsom said, "No president should be able to sell a pardon. Today, I’m calling for sweeping federal reform of the presidential pardon power. The Justice Department is not Donald Trump’s personal law firm. Justice is NOT for sale."In a video message accompanying the post, Newsom criticised MAGA supremo for delivering remarks at the department of justice (DOJ) alongside Attorney General Pam Bondi, who previously served as his personal defence lawyer."Today, Donald Trump is once again standing inside the Department of Justice next to his former personal defence lawyer, who is now the Attorney General, giving a speech about protecting American families," Newsom said.Questioning Trump's record on criminal justice, Newsom referred to the 1989 case involving five Black and Latino teenagers who were wrongfully accused of raping and assaulting a woman in New York's Central Park.The teenagers, later known as the Central Park Five, were exonerated after DNA evidence and a confession by another individual established their innocence."In 1989, you took out full-page ads screaming for the death penalty for five Black and Latino teenagers before a trial, before a shred of evidence. They were innocent. DNA proved it. You never apologised," Newsom said.The California governor also defended his own clemency decisions, insisting that individuals on the state's former death row would remain behind bars for life."To the families standing with him today, your grief is real. That's why every person, every person on California's former death row will die in prison. No one walks out," he said, contrasting his approach with Trump's use of presidential pardons.Newsom alleged that several individuals convicted of serious offences had received presidential pardons after making financial contributions or benefiting from personal connections involving Trump's political circle.Citing specific cases, he alleged that a billionaire facing bribery charges had secured a pardon after his family arranged a $50 million deal involving Trump's lawyer. He also claimed that an individual convicted of stealing $10 million from nursing home workers received clemency after his mother attended a million-dollar dinner at Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.Newsom also criticised Trump's decision to pardon former Blackwater security contractors convicted in connection with the 2007 killing of 14 Iraqi civilians, including two children, in Baghdad.He further referred to the pardon of a participant in the January 6 Capitol riot who subsequently pleaded guilty to soliciting what he believed was a 15-year-old girl for sex. Newsom also criticised Trump's pardon of a foreign leader accused of facilitating large-scale cocaine trafficking into the United States."Nearly two billion, nearly $2 billion owed to victims and their families, gone. His own pardon attorney said it out loud: 'No MAGA left behind'," Newsom alleged.Accusing Trump of applying different standards of justice based on an individual's wealth and political connections, Newsom said, "Donald Trump doesn't oppose mercy. He sells it. If you're poor, Black, or Brown, you get the needle. If you're rich and know Donald Trump, you get a pardon and a personal phone call."He also raised concerns over Trump's remarks suggesting that more pardons could be forthcoming, including his statement that the possibility of pardoning himself was not unreasonable."A Justice Department that prosecutes his enemies and pardons himself and his friends? That's not law enforcement. That's a protection racket," Newsom said.Calling for structural changes to presidential clemency powers, Newsom said reforms were needed to prevent future presidents from using their constitutional authority to grant pardons for personal or financial benefit."We need foundational federal reform, starting with this: no president can ever again turn the power of mercy into a business. No president and no one should be able to sell a pardon," he said.Concluding his video message, the California governor reiterated that the Justice Department must function independently and serve the American people."A Justice Department is not Donald Trump's law firm. Justice is not for sale--not in California, and not in America," Newsom added.Newsom's remarks came after Trump sharply criticised the California Governor over his decision to grant clemency to 548 death row inmates, including individuals convicted of murdering children.Speaking at the Department of Justice on Monday (local time), Trump described Newsom's decision as one of the most shocking acts of injustice in the country. He accused the Governor and what he termed the Radical Left of prioritising convicted criminals over victims and their families."We're here today to talk about one of the most shocking acts of injustice our country has ever seen... Just days ago, the Governor of California, Gavin Newsom, granted clemency and mercy to 548 of the most EVIL monsters on the face of the Earth," Trump said.The US President also announced a Presidential Directive ordering the DOJ to seek the death penalty for individuals convicted of murdering children, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims."I will sign a Presidential Directive ordering the DOJ to seek the death penalty for child murderers, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims. My order also directs the Attorney General to expedite the execution of federal death sentences. Once juries have spoken, capital punishment will be swift and certain," Trump said.He also referred to an executive order signed on the first day of his administration, directing the DOJ to pursue capital punishment for individuals convicted of murdering law enforcement officers.Trump further announced nearly $150 million in public safety grants to support the recruitment of more than 1,000 additional sworn law enforcement officers and improve responses to domestic violence and sexual assault cases.Additionally, he backed a legislative proposal introduced by Representative Brandon Gill, titled the 'Just Punishment for Murder Act'.The proposal seeks to strengthen capital punishment provisions and expand their application to individuals convicted of murdering law enforcement officers and illegal immigrants accused of murder.
Article Summary: California governor Gavin Newsom has called for sweeping federal reforms to the US president's power to grant pardons. He accused President Donald Trump of using the Justice Department to protect wealthy allies and politically connected individuals. Newsom's remarks came after Trump sharply criticised the California Governor over his decision to grant clemency to 548 death row inmates.

Article Title: China launches Shenzhou-24 spacecraft carrying first Pakistani astronaut to its space station, 90 experiments planned
Article Text:
A Long March 2F Y24 rocket carrying the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft with Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, blasts off to China's Tiangong space station

More than 90 experiments planned

China-Pakistan space cooperation

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

China targets crewed Moon landing by 2030

China on Wednesday successfully launched its Shenzhou-24 spacecraft carrying three astronauts, including Pakistani national Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, marking the first time a foreign astronaut has travelled aboard a Chinese mission to its Tiangong space station.The spacecraft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, carrying Ali, 40, alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39. The mission marks the first joint spaceflight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's crewed space programme.Ali, a former Pakistan Air Force pilot, will serve as a payload specialist during the mission. He is expected to conduct scientific experiments and technology tests alongside the Chinese crew before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, according to Chinese state media.Speaking ahead of the launch, Ali described the mission as the beginning of a broader journey in space exploration and cooperation between the two countries.“It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights,” he said in Mandarin.In English, he said the mission “is not a finish line” but a long path, expressing hope that future cooperation would expand from individual astronauts travelling together to multiple joint missions and eventually journeys to the Moon, Mars and beyond.“To every child who’s watching while I’m in orbit: Look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams," he said.The three-member crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during the mission, China's official Xinhua news agency reported.According to state broadcaster CCTV, Ali will undertake four scientific projects covering biotechnology and materials science. One of the experiments will involve photosynthetic microorganisms, including cyanobacteria.Ali's mission will be relatively short, and he is scheduled to return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, CCTV reported.For Tang, the mission will mark his third visit to the Tiangong space station, making him the first Chinese astronaut to travel there three times. Wu and Ali will be undertaking their first spaceflights.Tang said differences in language, culture and psychology had made preparations for the mission more challenging, but both teams had worked to overcome them.“The labels and operating instructions aboard the spacecraft and space station are all in Chinese, and the Pakistani astronaut began training with virtually no foundation of the language,” he said, adding that he and Wu had also stepped up their English studies.The mission is part of a space cooperation agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025. It marks a new phase in the two countries' growing partnership in space exploration and technology.Their cooperation has already included Chinese-launched Pakistani satellites, a joint satellite-navigation system and plans for a Pakistani-built lunar rover to fly aboard China's Chang'e mission around 2028.Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif extended his wishes to the astronauts ahead of the launch, describing the mission as a milestone in bilateral relations.“Tomorrow, Pakistan will look to the skies with anticipation, pride and deep gratitude,” he wrote on X.Praising Chinese President Xi Jinping, Sharif said his “visionary leadership and steadfast commitment to Pakistan-China friendship have taken our All-Weather Strategic Cooperative Partnership to unprecedented heights.”He also credited Pakistani scientists, the armed forces and national institutions for their contributions to the country's space programme.“Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space,” he said.China's space programme has expanded rapidly as Beijing seeks to strengthen its position in space exploration and compete with the United States.The country is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030, while NASA is targeting 2028 for its next astronaut landing on the Moon.Since Yuri Gagarin's first human spaceflight in 1961, citizens of around 50 countries have travelled to space. However, only three countries, Russia, the United States and China, have developed the capability to launch their own crewed spacecraft.
Article Summary: Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali is the first foreign astronaut to travel aboard a Chinese mission to its Tiangong space station. The spacecraft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, carrying Ali, 40, alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39. Ali will serve as a payload specialist during the mission.

Article Title: New Haven agrees to pay $30 million to George Gould, who spent nearly 27 years in prison, and the estate of Ronald Taylor, who died in 2011, after their convictions in a 1993 murder were thrown out
Article Text:
New Haven's $30 million settlement awaits committee review and Board of Alders approval for borrowing.

Two men convicted in a 1993 murder

A lengthy legal battle before exoneration

$30 million settlement and approval process

Wrongful-conviction settlements reach $77 million

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

More lawsuits remain unresolved

Nearly three decades behind bars, a conviction that unravelled years later and a settlement worth millions of dollars have brought two wrongful-conviction cases in Connecticut closer to a conclusion. The city of New Haven has agreed to pay $30 million to George Gould and the estate of Ronald Taylor, who were imprisoned for a 1993 murder they did not commit. While Gould will receive $18 million after spending almost 27 years incarcerated, Taylor's estate is set to receive $12 million following his death in 2011. The settlement, reported by the New Haven Independent and Hartford Courant, marks another major financial resolution for the city as it faces mounting lawsuits linked to wrongful convictions dating back several decades.Gould and Taylor were convicted of felony murder and other charges in connection with the July 4, 1993, killing of Eugenia Vega inside her Grand Avenue bodega in New Haven.According to the New Haven Independent, the prosecution's case relied heavily on testimony from a woman who claimed to have witnessed the crime. She later revealed that she had been arrested for prostitution and interrogated while experiencing severe heroin withdrawal.She alleged that police offered to help her obtain heroin in exchange for providing the statement they wanted. Investigators reportedly found no physical evidence linking either Gould or Taylor to the killing.Years later, two relatives reportedly approached the FBI and said Vega's son had confessed to them that he had killed his father, bringing fresh scrutiny to the convictions.The men's legal struggle involved multiple court proceedings. In 2010, a Connecticut Superior Court judge granted their habeas corpus petitions on grounds of actual innocence and ordered their release.However, the state appealed, and the Connecticut Supreme Court subsequently overturned that decision. During a second habeas proceeding, their petitions were denied, the online report adds.Gould returned to prison in 2011, while Taylor was allowed to remain at home because of his terminal cancer diagnosis. He died in October 2011, after spending more than 16 years incarcerated, New Haven Independent reported.Gould continued challenging his conviction and was released in 2021 after a judge modified his sentence. The state's Conviction Integrity Unit later reviewed the case, and prosecutors moved to vacate both convictions in 2024.The agreement was reached on November 13 in two consolidated federal civil rights cases against the city, the report added.Under the settlement, Gould will receive $18 million, while Taylor's estate, administered by Mary Murphy-Taylor, will receive $12 million. The latter payment remains subject to approval by the New Haven Probate Court.According to the Hartford Courant, the agreement also requires approval from the city's Litigation Settlement Committee. The New Haven Board of Alders must subsequently approve borrowing for the settlement.The New Haven Independent reported that Gould's legal representatives include Neufeld Scheck Brustin Hoffmann & Freudenberger, the Law Offices of Richard Emanuel and the Law Office of Attorney Michael A. Jefferson.The latest agreement represents the fourth and fifth federal civil rights lawsuits New Haven has settled within three months. Earlier settlements involved Adam Carmon for $16.5 million, Vernon Horn for $15.25 million and Marquis Jackson for $15.25 million.Together, the five settlements total $77 million. According to city officials cited by the New Haven Independent and Hartford Courant, borrowing to finance the payments could result in at least $116 million in repayments over 20 years when interest is included.Mayor Justin Elicker has acknowledged the city's responsibility to address past injustices while raising concerns about the financial burden on taxpayers. He has also called for the state to share more of the costs, noting that state authorities appealed the original decision granting Gould and Taylor relief.The mayor's office has pointed to the city's lack of insurance coverage for this type of incident in 1993 and the financial implications of settling claims decades later.The financial consequences may not end with the latest agreement. According to the New Haven Independent, lawsuits involving former Alder Troy Streater and Charles Coleman Jr. remain outstanding, alongside the separate case involving Stefon Morant, in which a jury previously awarded $38 million against the city. New Haven is appealing that verdict.For Gould, the settlement brings an end to a legal struggle that continued long after his release. For Taylor's family, the compensation comes years after his death and the eventual overturning of his conviction.The agreement represents another step in addressing wrongful convictions from New Haven's past, while leaving the city to confront the continuing legal and financial consequences.Image Courtesy: George Gould (right), with the late Ronald Taylor (center). Credit: Thomas MacMillan photo
Article Summary: The city of New Haven has agreed to pay $30 million to George Gould and the estate of Ronald Taylor, who were imprisoned for a 1993 murder they did not commit. Gould will receive $18 million after spending almost 27 years incarcerated, while Taylor's estate is set to receive $12 million following his death in 2011. The settlement marks another major financial resolution for the city as it faces mounting lawsuits linked to wrongful convictions dating back several decades.

Article Title: A Wisconsin Army veteran went to a Craig Morgan concert expecting a night of music; instead, Michael King and his family learned they would receive a new mortgage-free home, with a groundbreaking plan
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A country music concert in Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin, turned into an unexpected celebration for Army veteran Michael King and his family after they were selected to receive a custom-built home without a mortgage. The surprise announcement came during a benefit performance by country singer Craig Morgan on November 19, with local builder Belman Homes and nonprofit organisation Operation Finally Home joining forces for the project. WISN 12 News and Spectrum News 1 reported that the family had no idea they had already been chosen when they arrived at the event. King attended the concert with his wife, Marissa, and their two children, believing they were there as guests of the nonprofit. The family had expected to participate in an interview the following day as part of the selection process for a potential home. Instead, they discovered that the decision had already been made in their favour.The announcement was delivered by David Belman, president of Belman Homes, alongside Molly Halliday, senior vice president of Operation Finally Home. The organisations confirmed that the family would receive a new home in Waukesha, with a groundbreaking ceremony scheduled for November 20.For King, the announcement carried particular significance given the challenges he has faced since leaving military service. He enlisted in the US Army at 19 in 2004 and served as an infantryman until 2007. During his military career, he was stationed in Germany before being deployed to Kuwait and Iraq in support of combat operations.His service has left him living with several lasting health conditions, including service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), tinnitus and hearing loss. These challenges have continued to affect his everyday life, with his wife and children providing support as the family navigates the long-term effects of his military experience.The home will be built through a partnership between Belman Homes, a Wisconsin-based residential construction company, and Operation Finally Home, a Texas-based nonprofit dedicated to supporting military families and first responders. Founded in 2005, Operation Finally Home works with builders, developers, suppliers and community partners to provide mortgage-free homes, transitional housing and home modifications to veterans, first responders and surviving spouses.According to Spectrum News 1, the organisation has worked on more than 500 projects across 41 states since its establishment.The initiative aims to address housing challenges faced by individuals and families who have experienced significant sacrifices through military or emergency service. Rather than providing temporary assistance alone, its projects are designed to offer long-term stability through accessible and customised housing. Morgan’s involvement also added another connection to military service at the event. The country singer served in the US Army and Army Reserve for 17 years and reenlisted in the Reserves in 2023, according to Spectrum News 1.The Waukesha project is not the first collaboration between Belman Homes and Operation Finally Home in the area. In 2018, the organisations worked together to provide Army Staff Sergeant Mario Joe Davis and his family with a mortgage-free, accessible ranch-style home in the Town of Waukesha. Davis had medically retired after 11 years of service and was living with Parkinson’s disease. For the King family, however, the latest announcement marks the beginning of a new chapter. What they expected to be an ordinary evening of country music instead became the moment they learned they would have a permanent home without the financial burden of a mortgage.
Article Summary: Army veteran Michael King and his family were selected to receive a custom-built home without a mortgage. The surprise announcement came during a benefit performance by country singer Craig Morgan on November 19. The family had no idea they had already been chosen when they arrived at the event.

Article Title: Iowa residents told to take shelter as US Army prepares to detonate 5 tonnes of explosives; toxic dust feared
Article Text:
A sign is displayed for the United States Army's Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, Monday, Nov. 23, 2026.

Residents warned as toxic dust could spread across states

Court allows Army to proceed despite environmental concerns

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Residents of a small town in Iowa are being asked to take shelter indoors and keep their windows shut as the US Army prepares to detonate nearly five tonnes of unstable explosives at a nearby military ammunition plant on Wednesday, raising fears of toxic lead dust spreading across parts of the state and neighbouring Missouri.The controlled blast, scheduled for around 10 am ET, will destroy 9,700lb (4,400kg) of lead azide, a highly volatile compound used in military ammunition and explosives, stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a southeastern Iowa town with around 400 residents.The explosion could release plumes of toxic lead dust across a 100-mile (160km) radius. The projected path of the airborne material has shifted with changing weather conditions. The Army's latest forecast indicates that the plume could move southwest of Middletown and extend into northern Missouri.In a public safety advisory, the Army urged people in affected areas, particularly children, pregnant women and those with chronic illnesses, to avoid outdoor activities until further guidance is issued."A more precise time will be communicated after evaluating changing weather patterns and waiting for the safest possible conditions," the Army said on Tuesday.According to CNN, Army officials maintain that a controlled detonation is the safest available option because the lead azide has deteriorated and become dangerously unstable. Officials warned that colder temperatures or attempts to open the containers for chemical neutralisation could trigger an uncontrolled explosion.Authorities have advised people living within 20 miles of the ammunition plant to remain indoors with windows closed to reduce exposure to airborne lead dust, noise and vibration. Some residents within five miles southwest of the facility could also be asked to evacuate.The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) is supporting temporary relocation for residents of Middletown and surrounding areas considered at risk.FEMA administrator Cameron Hamilton said residents in the southwest direction had been offered relocation assistance, including transportation, accommodation, meals and other essential services.Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds has also declared a disaster emergency in Des Moines, Lee and Van Buren counties. The Iowa National Guard is preparing to deploy up to 100 soldiers to assist with public safety and community outreach.The operation was initially scheduled for last Friday but was postponed three times amid growing public opposition and legal challenges from environmental groups.The planned detonation faced a legal challenge over concerns that the explosion could disperse toxic lead dust and create long-term environmental and health risks.A three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit ruled on Monday that the Army could proceed with the operation, allowing an emergency permit issued by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to remain in place. The court found that the EPA had incorporated safeguards aimed at minimising the spread of dust.CNN reported that an attorney representing one of the environmental groups involved in the lawsuit said the legal battle was not entirely over.Michael Schmidt, an attorney with the Iowa Environmental Council, told CNN's Kaitlan Collins that the lawsuit had questioned the adequacy of the EPA's emergency permit, including provisions for the aftermath of the explosion and the clean-up process.At a press conference on Tuesday, acting US Army Secretary Adam Telle said officials had been unable to identify a viable alternative to destroying the unstable material."There is consensus across experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to an uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance," Telle said.Senator-elect Josh Turek criticised the circumstances that led to the chemicals deteriorating to such a dangerous condition, saying there had been a failure of transparency and communication.The Army has maintained that the controlled blast is necessary to eliminate the risk posed by the unstable stockpile.
Article Summary: US Army preparing to detonate nearly five tonnes of unstable explosives at a nearby military ammunition plant on Wednesday. Controlled blast will destroy 9,700lb (4,400kg) of lead azide, a highly volatile compound used in military ammunition and explosives. The explosion could release plumes of toxic lead dust across a 100-mile (160km) radius.

Article Title: 77-year-old Florida man arrested for feeding raccoons; insists the food was meant for 7 stray cats he had cared for over 16 years, which became his family after his son's death in 2010
Article Text:
Florida man's efforts to care for seven stray cats began in 2010

Dispute with wildlife authorities over raccoons

Why was the Florida man arrested ?

Man disputes the allegations

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A 77-year-old man in Jacksonville, Florida, was arrested after wildlife officers accused him of illegally feeding raccoons, but he insists the food was meant for seven stray cats he and his wife have cared for over 16 years. Louis Abbruzze, who owns a warehouse on Youngerman Court, says the cats became an important part of their lives after they lost their only son in 2010. He has been leaving the warehouse door slightly open at night so the animals can come inside, eat and shelter from the weather. However, the arrangement eventually attracted the attention of wildlife authorities, who said raccoons were also gathering around the property and consuming the food.Abbruzze and his wife began looking after stray cats around their warehouse following the death of their only son in 2010. He described caring for the animals as something that helped the couple cope with their loss.Over the years, they trapped the cats, arranged vaccinations and sterilisation, and found homes for several of them. Seven cats remain at the warehouse, where Abbruzze says they continue to receive food and shelter.He described the animals as more than just strays, saying they had become like children to him and his wife. He also credited them with helping the couple find a renewed sense of purpose after their personal tragedy.The disagreement reportedly began around a year and a half before his arrest, when the property's homeowners association hired new management. According to Abbruzze, the management objected to him leaving the warehouse door open at night and warned that he could face fines or legal action if he continued.Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) officers had also raised concerns about raccoons gathering around the property. Abbruzze said he had previously been warned about leaving food outside and believed he was following the authorities' instructions by feeding the cats and removing the food whenever raccoons appeared.However, the FWC said officers had received complaints about a tenant feeding raccoons and that Abbruzze had previously been cited for providing the animals with food and access to his unit.According to an officer's report cited by USA Today Network, approximately 10 to 15 raccoons were waiting near the back door of the business when the officer arrived.FWC officers arrested Abbruzze on September 15, 2026, on a misdemeanour charge related to feeding wildlife. The arrest followed earlier citations over the same issue.According to Jacksonville Sheriff's Office booking information cited by USA Today Network, he had previously been documented for the same violation three times.Florida law prohibits intentionally feeding certain wildlife, including raccoons, or placing food and rubbish in a manner that attracts them. Under Florida Statutes Section 379.412, repeat violations can result in criminal penalties.The restrictions are intended to prevent wild animals from becoming dependent on human food, losing their natural fear of people or gathering in residential and commercial areas, where they can create safety and property-related problems.Abbruzze maintains that he never intended to feed raccoons and that his actions were solely aimed at looking after the seven cats. He also described the circumstances of his arrest, saying officers handcuffed him despite his difficulty walking with a broken ankle and a cane.Speaking about the incident, he questioned why he was being treated like a criminal when, according to him, he was simply trying to care for animals.He said he expected to return to court with his attorney the following week.The FWC, meanwhile, maintains that feeding raccoons is prohibited under Florida regulations, regardless of whether other animals are also being fed at the same location.
Article Summary: Louis Abbruzze and his wife began looking after stray cats around their warehouse following the death of their only son in 2010. He has been leaving the warehouse door slightly open at night so the animals can come inside, eat and shelter from the weather. The arrangement attracted the attention of wildlife authorities, who said raccoons were also gathering around the property and consuming the food.

Article Title: A North Carolina couple lost their 18-year-old daughter in a car crash; 22 years later, they are honouring her memory by rescuing hundreds of orphaned and injured animals through a wildlife centre nam
Article Text:
How the couple turned personal loss into a wildlife rescue mission

What happens at Holly's Nest Animal Rescue

Why orphaned fawns make up a major part of their work

Their home has become an extension of the rescue centre

Thousands of acres provide a place for rescued animals to return

A demanding routine that can last 18 hours a day

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The goal is to return every animal to the wild

A couple in North Carolina, US, have turned an unimaginable personal tragedy into a mission to protect wildlife. Byron and Kim Wortham lost their 18-year-old daughter, Holly, in a car crash in February 2004. More than two decades later, they are keeping her memory alive through Holly's Nest Animal Rescue, a wildlife rehabilitation centre they established in her honour. The facility takes in injured, abandoned and orphaned animals, nurses them back to health and releases them into suitable natural habitats. From baby deer whose mothers have been killed on roads to injured owls, raccoons and foxes, the couple's work has grown into a demanding commitment to wildlife conservation, with the centre now caring for hundreds of animals each year.Holly Wortham was 18 and in her final year of high school when she died in a car accident in February 2004. She was remembered by her family as an artist and an animal lover. Her death deeply affected her parents and their three other children.In the years that followed, Kim struggled with the loss and found it difficult to return to her previous routine. She eventually left her job at a library. Caring for animals gradually became a way for her to reconnect with the world and find purpose after the tragedy.Byron and Kim began obtaining the necessary permits to rehabilitate small mammals, including squirrels, rabbits and opossums. What started as an effort to honour Holly's affection for animals gradually developed into a dedicated wildlife rescue operation. They named it Holly's Nest to ensure that their daughter's memory remained at the centre of their work.Located near Sanford in Lee County, North Carolina, Holly's Nest is a wildlife rehabilitation facility that receives animals from members of the public, wildlife officers and other rehabilitators.Its work involves rescuing injured, abandoned and orphaned animals, providing medical attention and specialised care, and preparing them for release once they can survive independently.The centre looks after a wide range of native wildlife, including white-tailed deer, raccoons, foxes, opossums, squirrels, rabbits, beavers, owls, hawks and other birds. Some animals arrive with serious injuries, while others are too young to survive without human intervention.The facility has also cared for animals with unusual conditions, including an albino fawn, a dwarf raccoon and a disabled squirrel.One of the centre's biggest responsibilities is caring for white-tailed deer, particularly fawns separated from their mothers after road accidents. According to a June 2026 report by The News & Observer, Holly's Nest has become North Carolina's largest deer rehabilitation facility, taking in an average of around 150 fawns annually.During the busiest part of the season, the centre can receive five to eight new fawns a day for about a month. On June 5, 2026, approximately 50 fawns were being cared for at the facility.Some arrive in particularly distressing circumstances, including newborns whose mothers have been struck by vehicles shortly after giving birth. The young deer require regular bottle-feeding and close attention until they are strong enough to survive without human care.The Worthams' commitment to wildlife rehabilitation extends well beyond the centre's outdoor enclosures. Over the years, animals requiring special attention have also been cared for inside their home.A beaver named Bucky once occupied a bathtub in the bathroom that had belonged to Holly. He even attempted to build a dam there. Baby raccoons have been seen resting in hammocks, while young foxes have slept in dog beds. The couple has also cared for animals in their basement, particularly those requiring cooler conditions.The household has included two macaws named Jimmy Buffett and Bruce Springsteen. Kim has spoken about her affection for beavers, describing their behaviour as similar to that of children.These unusual arrangements reflect the demands of looking after animals that cannot immediately be placed in outdoor rehabilitation enclosures.Rehabilitation is only one part of the couple's conservation work. Finding suitable habitats where recovered animals can be released is equally important.According to The News & Observer, Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of Epic Games, provided Holly's Nest with access to approximately 8,000 acres of land for wildlife releases. The protected areas give rehabilitated animals an opportunity to return to natural surroundings rather than being released into unsuitable or heavily developed locations.The arrangement has been particularly valuable for animals that need appropriate habitat to survive independently. For the Worthams, the ultimate objective is not to keep rescued wildlife in captivity but to give it a chance to return to the wild.Running the rehabilitation centre requires considerable time and physical effort. During the busiest months, the couple can spend as many as 18 hours a day feeding animals, cleaning enclosures, preparing food and attending to new arrivals.April through October is particularly demanding because many young animals need assistance during this period. The couple prepares different diets depending on the species, with food including fruit, oats and other suitable provisions.Byron also takes their conservation message beyond the facility. He conducts wildlife education programmes at schools, parks, veterans' facilities and community venues, helping people understand the challenges faced by native animals.The centre's work is supported by donations, volunteers and the couple's own contributions. The 2024 report stated that Holly's Nest did not receive federal, state or local government funding and relied on donations and personal resources to meet its expenses.Despite the care and attention the animals receive, the Worthams believe that successful rehabilitation should ultimately lead to freedom. Their aim is to help wildlife recover sufficiently to survive in its natural environment rather than remain dependent on humans.Byron has expressed this philosophy through a simple belief: "five minutes of freedom is better than a lifetime of captivity".The couple's work has therefore become more than a tribute to their daughter. Through Holly's Nest, they are helping injured and orphaned wildlife recover, while also giving animals that have lost their natural habitats or mothers another opportunity to survive.For Byron and Kim, every animal that returns to the wild represents another way of keeping Holly's love for nature alive.
Article Summary: Byron and Kim Wortham lost their 18-year-old daughter, Holly, in a car crash in 2004. Caring for animals gradually became a way for her to reconnect with the world and find purpose after the tragedy. More than two decades later, they are keeping her memory alive through Holly's Nest Animal Rescue, a wildlife rehabilitation centre they established in her honour.

Article Title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose deportation sparked legal battle for Trump admin, leaves US for Spain voluntarily
Article Text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia and his wife Jennifer Vasquez Sura depart the US District Court on the day of a hearing in his case, in Greenbelt, Maryland, US, October 6, 2026.

How Garcia became the face of Trump's deportation crackdown

Trump administration wanted to deport him to African countries

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant who was mistakenly deported to El Salvador by the Trump administration despite a court order protecting him from removal, has voluntarily left the United States for Spain, his lawyers and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed on Tuesday. His deportation in March 2025 had triggered a major legal battle and drawn widespread criticism of the administration's immigration crackdown.The 31-year-old reached an agreement with federal authorities to leave the US voluntarily rather than face another forced deportation. CNN reported that Garcia travelled to Spain on a commercial flight along with his American wife and attorney.The advocacy group We Are CASA, which has supported Garcia and his family, also confirmed his departure, saying he had "walked out of the United States a free man". According to the organisation, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents removed his ankle monitor at the airport.Garcia is now expected to undertake international speaking engagements in several countries.Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, who had campaigned for Garcia's release and met him at a prison in El Salvador last year, welcomed the development."A year and a half ago, the Trump administration wanted to leave Kilmar Abrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag.Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man – unharmed and with dignity," Van Hollen said in a statement.Garcia's case became a major flashpoint in the Trump administration's immigration crackdown after he was deported to El Salvador in March 2025, despite an immigration judge's earlier order preventing his removal to the country.He had entered the US illegally as a teenager around 2011 and had been living in Maryland with his American wife and child. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because a gang there had threatened him and his family.Although he was allowed to live and work in the US under ICE supervision, he was not granted permanent residency.Despite the protection order, US authorities arrested Garcia in Baltimore and deported him to El Salvador, where he was detained at Cecot, a notorious mega-prison. The Trump administration subsequently acknowledged in court documents that his deportation had happened because of an administrative error.A federal judge ordered the government to work towards bringing him back to the US, but the administration resisted for months. Garcia was eventually returned to American soil in June 2025 after the US reached an arrangement with El Salvador.However, his return was followed by another legal battle. He was arrested on human-smuggling charges in Tennessee, but a federal judge dismissed the case in May 2026, citing what was described as a "tainted investigation". The Justice Department has appealed the ruling.Even after Garcia returned to the US, the Trump administration continued pursuing his removal, proposing several African countries as possible destinations.Officials had considered Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and, most recently, Liberia for his deportation. Garcia had previously expressed a preference for Costa Rica, which had indicated it could offer him some form of legal status.However, conditions imposed by the federal judge who dismissed his criminal case prevented him from voluntarily travelling there.According to CNN, the administration continued its efforts to arrange third-country deportations even as Garcia challenged his removal in court. The dispute took another turn in October, when a scheduled court hearing on his possible deportation to Liberia was abruptly cancelled after lawyers for both sides left the courtroom with Garcia.The latest agreement allows him to leave the US voluntarily for Spain, avoiding another forced removal.Van Hollen said he was relieved that Garcia would be able to live in a country of his choice and remain free from what he described as the administration's constant persecution.
Article Summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant who was mistakenly deported to El Salvador by the Trump administration, has voluntarily left the United States for Spain. His deportation in March 2025 had triggered a major legal battle and drawn widespread criticism of the administration's immigration crackdown. The 31-year-old reached an agreement with federal authorities to leave the US voluntarily rather than face another forced deportation.

Article Title: Trump called Abdul El-Sayed a 'jihadist' during midterms, now he wants to meet him over Trumpcare
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump
