US President Donald Trump has said he intends to meet Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed to discuss the Democrat’s proposal for universal healthcare, after unexpectedly endorsing his suggestion to brand the plan as “Trumpcare”.In an interview with the New York Post on Tuesday, Trump described El-Sayed as a “smart guy” and praised his decision to associate the president’s name with the healthcare proposal. He also suggested that the two could find common ground despite their political differences.“He’s a smart guy. He did a good job. He actually did a very good job,” Trump told the newspaper during a 45-minute interview at the Oval Office.“I know I’ll be meeting with him. Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go,” he added.El-Sayed, who made universal healthcare a central issue during his Senate campaign, proposed renaming his Medicare for All plan “Trumpcare” earlier this month. He shared an image of a gold-coloured healthcare card bearing the name on X and challenged Trump to support a system that would provide healthcare coverage “from cradle to grave”.Trump drew attention to the proposal on Saturday by reposting a screenshot of El-Sayed’s post.During Tuesday’s interview, he described the branding idea as “very smart”, according to the New York Post.The president also indicated that he was open to working with Democrats in Congress, although he predicted that negotiations could begin with disagreements. Democrats are set to control both chambers of Congress during the final two years of Trump’s presidency.“I’m just going to veto everything there is, and then at some point I think they’re going to want to negotiate. I will, and we can do health care. We can do a lot of great things together,” Trump said.The proposed meeting marks a change in tone after months of hostility between the two during the midterm election campaign.Trump repeatedly targeted El-Sayed at rallies, at one point referring to him as “Mohammed” and falsely describing the former public health official as a “jihadist”.Trump had earlier warned that an El-Sayed victory would be “a devastating blow for our country”.The Democrat also frequently criticised Trump and Vice President JD Vance during his campaign. Responding to attacks over his name and faith, El-Sayed said these issues were not responsible for the financial pressures facing ordinary Americans.“They can keep saying my name. They can keep pointing to my faith. My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your groceries,” he said in the closing days of the race.Despite the exchanges, El-Sayed has indicated that he is willing to meet the president if doing so could help advance his legislative priorities. Speaking on ABC’s This Week earlier this month, he said he would be open to discussions with Trump or other political figures, irrespective of party affiliation.“I’ve never met the man. He is the president of the United States. I am the US senator-elect from the state of Michigan. I am happy to meet with him, like I’ll meet with anyone who can advance the goals I ran on to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for all,” El-Sayed said.The office of Vice President Vance also confirmed last week that it had started contacting the incoming senator after learning he wanted to meet with the administration.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has said he intends to meet Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed to discuss the Democrat's proposal for universal healthcare. In an interview with the New York Post on Tuesday, Trump described the Democrat as a ‘smart guy’ and suggested that the two could find common ground. The proposed meeting marks a change in tone after months of hostility between the two.

Article Title: An Illinois property owner faced $53,000 in additional fines over scrap vehicles, pallets and other debris on his land; appeals court vacates fines but upholds nuisance finding
Article Text:
Representative image generated using AI

Legal complications with the city

What the appeals court found

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

An Illinois appeals court has cancelled about $53,000 in daily fines against a Mattoon man, as the city never charged him for the days it sought to penalise him. However, the court upheld the finding that his two properties on Broadway Avenue were a public nuisance, along with the original $750 fine.The Fifth District Appellate Court issued the opinion on Monday, 23 November, closing a case that began in 2018. Tim Quackenbush, who owns the properties, has run a demolition and excavation business since 1978. The city says his land became a dumping ground for scrap metal, wooden pallets, plastic totes, a hot tub and inoperable vehicles. Quackenbush argued that the materials were stock for his business and that the zoning allowed them.The city filed a complaint in September 2018, describing a day's worth of problems. In January 2020, a trial judge found that the properties were a nuisance and fined him $750. He could get the fine reduced to $100 if he cleaned up. However, he did not, at least not sufficiently. So the case remained open for years, with multiple hearings, two site visits and orders telling him what to fix. But progress remained slow.During a 2021 hearing, Quackenbush was asked if he had completed the cleanup.“Well, it depends on what you call done,” Quackenbush, the defendant, said. He told the court that he had cleaned up certain areas and was allowed to keep “all these items”. He added that he did not know why “the City seems to think that I have to put them in a certain order, or I have to get rid of a certain amount”.Back in 2019, the police chief stated that progress was “close to none”. As the properties remained messy, the judge added $50 a day for 101 days. In a January 2025 final order, the judge added another $50 for each of 959 days. Those additional fines brought the total to $53,750.The majority opinion focused on the wording of the city's rules rather than the state of the properties. The rules allow the city to issue a new ticket for each day a problem continues. However, they also say that fines can only be imposed for tickets the city has already issued. The city issued one ticket, so the court said it could only collect one fine.The court also observed that the additional fines were unfair, as Quackenbush had not been formally charged with those additional violations and had no opportunity to defend himself against them in court. The judges also noted that the trial judge had said the city could make him remove items but had never ordered him to do so. This made the fines appear more like a punishment than a means of cleaning up the property.The court agreed that the properties were a nuisance. Photos from the trial showed open tubs, barrels, a dumpster and piles of pallets. The judges agreed that these conditions were likely to attract insects and rats. The zoning argument did not work either. Land can be zoned for industrial use and still be a nuisance if it is not properly maintained, the court said.While Justice Barberis agreed that the properties were a nuisance, he disagreed with removing the $53,000 in fines. He read the city's general fine rules together with the nuisance rules. He pointed to a 2022 case from another Illinois appeals court that had interpreted similar city rules together. He also said the word “may” in the rules gave the city a choice, rather than an obligation, to issue a new ticket each day.Justice Barberis disagreed that the additional fines were unfair. He said the judge had fined the defendant only for specific periods supported by evidence, not for an unlimited number of days.He also said that six years of court hearings had given Quackenbush sufficient warning that he could face additional fines.The opinion is a draft, which means it may change before the court issues its final decision or considers a request for rehearing. For now, the court has removed the additional $53,000 in fines but retained the original $750 fine and the ruling that the properties were a public nuisance.
Article Summary: Tim Quackenbush, who owns the properties, has run a demolition and excavation business since 1978. The city says his land became a dumping ground for scrap metal, wooden pallets, plastic totes, a hot tub and inoperable vehicles. He argued that the materials were stock for his business and that the zoning allowed them.

Article Title: California woman bought a house in 1978 and left it to her partner through a trust; after both died, another woman challenged his son's claim to the property, but the court ruled in his favour
Article Text:
Representative image

How the California couple arranged their trusts

Why the house became part of a legal dispute

Another woman challenged the son's inheritance claim

Why the appeals court ruled in the son's favour

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What the ruling means for the property

A house purchased in 1978 by a California woman became the centre of an inheritance dispute decades later, after her death and that of her long-term partner. Diane Martinez had lived at the Stanton property with Lester Edmond Compton and named him as the sole beneficiary of her trust. However, the property had never been formally transferred into her trust through a deed. After Martinez died in 2020, a probate court recognised the house as an asset of her trust and transferred ownership to Lester. He died less than two months later, leaving his son, John Compton, to establish that the property belonged to his father's trust. Another woman challenged his claim, but an appeals court upheld his position on November 24, 2026.Martinez purchased the Stanton property in 1978 and subsequently lived there with Compton. More than three decades later, on September 12, 2012, the couple created separate trusts to organise their assets and specify who would receive their property.Under the Diane Marie Martinez Trust, Compton was named as the successor trustee and the sole beneficiary of her estate. The separate Compton Trust named Lester as its trustee, Martinez as his first successor trustee and his son, John, as the second successor trustee.Lester's trust also contained an important provision stating that his worldly possessions were to be held for Martinez and, if she died before him, were to pass to John. Alongside this, Lester signed an assignment transferring all his property, including assets acquired in the future, to his trust.Although Martinez's trust identified the Stanton property, she never executed or recorded a deed formally transferring it into the trust. Consequently, the property remained in her name when she died on March 21, 2020.In June 2020, Compton filed a petition seeking an order confirming that the house should be transferred to him as successor trustee of Martinez's trust. On April 20, 2021, the probate court approved his request, declaring the property transferred to him and vesting both legal and equitable title in his name as successor trustee.Compton died on June 14, 2021, less than two months after obtaining the order. This brought the separate trust he had created with Martinez back into focus, particularly the clause covering property he might acquire after signing the document in 2012.In August 2022, John Compton approached the probate court seeking confirmation that his father's trust was valid, that he was its sole beneficiary and that the Stanton property belonged to the trust. He also sought authority to manage and control the property as its trustee.Cindy Lynn Cavanaugh objected to the petition in September 2023, arguing that the trust assignment did not adequately identify the house. She relied on California's statute of frauds, which sets requirements for written evidence establishing trusts involving real estate.Her argument was that Lester had not owned the Stanton property when he created his trust in 2012 and that a general assignment covering future property was insufficient to establish ownership of a specific house. The probate court rejected the objection after considering the trust documents, agreed facts, John's testimony and excerpts from Cavanaugh's deposition. It ruled that the property was an asset of Lester's trust, prompting Cavanaugh to appeal.The California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Three, examined whether Lester's signed assignment could cover a property he acquired years after creating his trust.The judges found that the document explicitly covered all his property, regardless of its type, location or when it was acquired. They also relied on the April 20, 2021 probate order, which had formally established that Lester owned the Stanton property as successor trustee of Martinez's trust.The court referred to an earlier California decision, Ukkestad v. RBS Asset Finance, Inc., which recognised that real estate can become part of a trust without a separate deed when the required written documentation and evidence identify the property.Applying that reasoning, the judges concluded that Lester's signed assignment, combined with the earlier probate order, was sufficient to establish that the Stanton house belonged to his trust. The court rejected Cavanaugh's arguments and affirmed the lower court's judgment on November 24, 2026.The appellate judgment leaves John Compton's claim to the Stanton property intact. As the sole beneficiary and successor trustee of his father's trust, he can manage and control the property as an asset of that trust.The court also ordered Cavanaugh to pay the respondent's costs of the appeal. However, the judgment did not specify the property's market value or award a separate monetary payment.The ruling also does not establish that Cavanaugh lived in the house or identify her relationship to Martinez or Compton. Its central finding concerns the validity of Lester's assignment of future-acquired property and whether the Stanton house consequently became part of his trust.
Article Summary: Diane Martinez lived at the Stanton property with Lester Edmond Compton. She named him as the sole beneficiary of her trust, but the property had never been formally transferred into her trust through a deed. After Martinez died in 2020, a probate court transferred ownership to Lester. He died less than two months later, leaving his son, John, to establish that the property belonged to his father's trust. Another woman challenged his claim, but an appeals court upheld his position.

Article Title: Five years after a nine-year-old boy died of brain cancer, his family fulfilled his wish by opening a 15,000-square-foot children's museum inside a hospital to give young patients a place to play
Article Text:
Image Courtesy: Kids Join The Fight

Why Walker dreamt of a Imaginarium

Inside the Imaginarium

How the family brought the idea to life

Contribution beyond the museum

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Some people, even after they are gone, leave such a profound mark on the world that their presence continues to be felt in the lives of people they never got to meet. For the Beery family, that legacy belongs to their nine-year-old son, Walker. Five years after losing him to brain cancer, his parents have fulfilled a wish he once made during his hospital stays: to give other children like him somewhere to play, explore and, even for a little while, forget that they are sick.On November 17, 2026, Manning Family Children's in New Orleans, Louisiana , celebrated the opening of Walker's Imaginarium, a 15,000-square-foot children's museum built within the hospital. It is believed to be the first museum of its kind to be incorporated into a children's hospital, transforming an idea that began with a little boy's longing for a happier hospital experience into a space that can now bring joy to thousands of young patients and their families.As reported by PEOPLE , Walker was just 7 years old when he was diagnosed with medulloblastoma, a rare and aggressive form of brain cancer, in August 2019. What followed was a difficult 2 year journey involving surgeries, lengthy hospital stays, chemotherapy and radiation. Yet, in the middle of everything he was going through, Walker was thinking about something beyond his own illness.During his time in hospital, he often wished there was somewhere he could go outside his room, get some fresh air and take a break from the endless cycle of treatments.His initial idea was a butterfly garden where children receiving care could spend time outdoors and enjoy a little distraction. It was a simple wish, but one that said a great deal about the little boy behind it. Even while dealing with an experience no child should have to endure, he wanted other children to have something to look forward to.Walker passed away in September 2021, aged 9. But his idea did not leave with him.In the years that followed, his parents, Taylor and Angel Beery, worked to turn his wish into something much bigger. Together with the nonprofit organisation Kids Join The Fight , which Walker helped establish, they began working towards creating a space where children receiving hospital care could experience the kind of joy that often gets pushed aside by illness.The result is a two-storey museum that feels a world away from the clinical surroundings of a hospital. And rather fittingly for a project born in New Orleans, the city itself has been woven into almost every corner of it.According to Good News Network , children entering the museum are welcomed by interactive lights, marching band music and percussion instruments arranged around a whimsical tree. There is even a year-round Mardi Gras parade, complete with a special float called the Krewe of Walker. An enormous LED butterfly hangs overhead, its wings moving in response to children playing on an accessible swing below it.Elsewhere, young visitors can explore an imaginative bayou, enjoy airboat rides, wander through a colourful forest or take part in a miniature sports field. There is also a lemonade stand and a playful recreation of Louisiana's famous front-porch culture, complete with a crawfish boil. For children who fancy something a little more competitive, an outdoor terrace houses a nine-hole miniature golf course inspired by local landmarks, including an oversized alligator and a fireworks display at the Superdome.But the museum is not just about running around and having fun. Its design takes into account that every child has different needs, particularly those who are undergoing treatment or have limited mobility. According to Manning Family Children's , the space includes wheelchair-accessible activities, sensory experiences and quieter areas where children and their families can simply sit together. The idea is to make play accessible to everyone, regardless of their physical or medical circumstances.There is also a dedicated classroom planned for the second floor, which will support children who miss out on school because of prolonged hospital stays. An interactive multimedia studio, developed in partnership with the Ryan Seacrest Foundation, is expected to open in February 2027.Speaking to PEOPLE , Walker's father, Taylor, said the family was proud that the promise they had made had finally been delivered. Recalling his son's approach to his illness, he shared that Walker never pretended things were easy. He simply refused to let the pain become the only thing that defined his experience.That thought seems to sit at the very heart of the project. As Lucio Fragoso, president and CEO of Manning Family Children's, explained in the hospital's announcement , while it may not always be possible to change why a child is admitted to hospital, it is possible to change what being there feels like.The project, which took five years of planning and construction, has been funded entirely through philanthropic contributions, with patient families, medical teams, architects and designers helping bring the idea to life. As reported by Becker's Hospital Review , Manning Family Children's has also become the first hospital to join the Association of Children's Museums, making the initiative an important step towards bringing the experience of a children's museum into healthcare settings.The family has also continued Walker's work beyond the museum. Through Kids Join The Fight , they support paediatric brain cancer research and provide financial assistance to families navigating childhood cancer. The organisation was founded to ensure that other children and their families have access to the support and resources they need during an incredibly difficult time.It is difficult to imagine a more beautiful way to honour a child's memory. What began as a little boy wishing for somewhere to escape his hospital room has become a 15,000-square-foot space where other children can make music, play games, discover new things and spend time with the people they love. The museum cannot undo what happened to Walker, nor can it make the experience of childhood illness any less difficult for the families who walk through its doors. But it can give them something that hospital corridors often leave little room for: ordinary childhood moments. And somewhere in between all those giggles and chatters, a 9-year old boy looks over smiling, seeing his Imaginarium exactly as he imagined.
Article Summary: Walker's Imaginarium is a 15,000-square-foot children's museum built within Manning Family Children's in New Orleans, Louisiana. It is believed to be the first museum of its kind to be incorporated into a children's hospital. Visitors can explore an imaginative bayou, enjoy airboat rides, wander through a colourful forest or take part in a miniature sports field.

Article Title: A man named two relatives as beneficiaries of a $746,000 life insurance policy during Idaho divorce proceedings, then died in a mining accident; on November 23, judges revived his wife's claim to a sh
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Husband named relatives as beneficiaries during divorce

State courts recognised wife's 50% interest

Appeals court explains how QDRO protection applies

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Ninth Circuit sends case back for further proceedings

A life insurance policy became the centre of a legal dispute after a man changed its beneficiaries while his divorce was pending and subsequently died in a mining accident. Although his estranged wife was not named on the policy, she argued that she was entitled to half of its proceeds because the insurance benefits were part of their marital property.In a November 23, 2026, decision in Ashlock v. Ashlock, the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit vacated a federal court judgment favouring the deceased man's relatives and reopened the wife's legal challenge. The ruling, available on Justia, held that a federal law exception allowing certain divorce-related orders to override Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) preemption can apply to employer-sponsored life insurance plans as well as pension plans. The court sent the case back for further proceedings to determine whether the wife's court orders qualify for that protection.Tina Ashlock and Jerry Ashlock married in 2009. Jerry filed for divorce in an Idaho state court in December 2020. During the proceedings, the court issued an injunction prohibiting either spouse from transferring property acquired during their marriage while the divorce case remained pending.In March 2021, Jerry started working for Stillwater Mining Company in Montana and enrolled in an employer-sponsored life insurance policy issued by Life Insurance Company of North America (LINA). Despite the injunction, he named his relatives, Mary Ashlock and Brad Wilt, as the policy's only beneficiaries.Jerry died in a mining accident in Montana in June 2021, before the divorce was finalised. Tina subsequently contacted LINA, claiming an interest in the insurance proceeds. The insurer rejected her claim because she was not named as a beneficiary and argued that ERISA prevented her from claiming the money under state community-property laws. In December 2021, LINA confirmed that it had distributed the entire $746,000 policy payout to Mary and Brad.Tina continued pursuing her claim through state courts. In September 2022, an Idaho court issued an order recognising her 50% community-property interest in the insurance proceeds. It also found that Jerry had violated the divorce-related injunction by naming his relatives as beneficiaries. The Idaho court deferred enforcement of Tina's interest to the Montana probate court, which subsequently adopted the findings and conclusions of the Idaho order and recognised her community-property interest.Tina then filed a federal lawsuit against Mary, Brad, LINA and Principal Life Insurance Company. She sought a declaration recognising her entitlement to the proceeds and alleged unjust enrichment against the two relatives. She also brought an ERISA claim against the insurer, alleging that it had improperly denied her benefits. However, in July 2024, the US District Court for the District of Arizona dismissed her claim against LINA. It later entered judgment in favour of Mary and Brad, agreeing with the argument that ERISA's exception for qualified domestic relations orders applied only to pension plans, not life insurance policies.Tina challenged the federal court's decision before the Ninth Circuit. The central question was whether ERISA's qualified domestic relations order (QDRO) exception could cover welfare benefit plans, including employer-sponsored life insurance. A QDRO is a domestic relations order that recognises another person's right to receive some or all of the benefits under an employee benefit plan. Such orders can protect a spouse's or former spouse's interests in benefits during divorce proceedings.The appeals court explained that ERISA recognises both pension plans and welfare benefit plans. The latter include employer-sponsored benefits providing accident, disability and death coverage. The judges held that the statutory language does not restrict the QDRO exception to pension plans. They also noted that several other federal appeals courts had previously reached the same interpretation.The Ninth Circuit vacated the federal district court's judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings. It instructed the lower court to determine whether Tina possesses a qualifying QDRO that entitles her to a share of the insurance proceeds.The November 23 ruling does not itself award Tina half of the $746,000 or order Mary and Brad to return the money. Instead, it establishes that the QDRO exception can apply to the type of life insurance plan involved, allowing her claim to be considered under the correct interpretation of federal law.
Article Summary: Tina Ashlock and Jerry Ashlock married in 2009. Jerry filed for divorce in an Idaho state court in December 2020. During the proceedings, the court issued an injunction prohibiting either spouse from transferring property acquired during their marriage while the divorce case remained pending. Jerry enrolled in an employer-sponsored life insurance policy. He named his relatives as the policy's only beneficiaries. He died in a mining accident in Montana in June 2021, before the divorce was finalised. Tina subsequently contacted LINA, claiming an interest in the insurance proceeds.

Article Title: An Arizona woman lived with her partner in the same Phoenix house for 24 years, but he never divorced his estranged wife; after his death, an appeals court upheld the legal wife's ownership of the hom
Article Text:
Court rules estranged wife owns Phoenix home, rejects partner's 24-year claim. (Representational photo)

Why the 24-year stay did not give her ownership

Court rejects demand for money spent on house

Appeals court upholds earlier ruling

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

An Arizona woman who spent 24 years living in a Phoenix house with her partner has failed to secure ownership of the property after his death. An appeals court has ruled in favour of his estranged wife, who had left the house nearly 25 years earlier but was still legally married to him.According to the judgement , the dispute centred on a house bought by Troy Torrence and Rita Mack in 1998. The couple purchased the Phoenix property together, with an arrangement that allowed the surviving owner to inherit the other's share.Their relationship broke down the following year, and Mack moved out. However, the couple never legally ended their marriage or changed the ownership arrangement for the house.In 2000, Dimica Hicks moved into the property with Torrence. She continued to live there until his death in September 2024. After his death, Hicks was appointed to handle his estate and approached the court seeking rights over the house.Hicks argued that her long stay at the property and financial contributions towards it gave her a claim to ownership. She also sought repayment for expenses related to the house. However, a lower court rejected her ownership claim and later refused her demand for compensation.The Arizona Court of Appeals has now upheld that decision. In a ruling filed on Monday, the court said Mack became the sole owner after Torrence's death because their joint ownership agreement remained in place.Hicks argued that she had lived in the house long enough to claim it through adverse possession, a legal route through which someone may acquire rights over property occupied for a specified period under certain conditions.But the court found that the circumstances of her stay did not support such a claim. Hicks had acknowledged that Torrence had allowed her to move into the house and live there.The court said this was important because her stay had begun with Torrence's permission. Her presence in the property did not establish that she had occupied it against Mack's ownership rights.It also found no evidence that the original joint ownership arrangement between Mack and Torrence had ever been ended. Nor could Hicks show that she had taken exclusive control of the house in a manner that would support her ownership claim.The fact that Mack had moved out did not automatically take away her rights over the property. Since she and Torrence had continued to own the house jointly, his death meant that his share passed to her.This left Mack as the sole owner, despite having moved out decades before Hicks began living there.Apart from seeking ownership, Hicks wanted Mack to repay money she said she had spent on the property. Her claims included contributions towards the mortgage, repairs and improvements, as well as other household expenses.The lower court, however, found that Hicks had not established that Mack had unfairly benefited from her spending. The appeals court agreed that there was no reason to overturn this finding.The earlier judgment noted that Torrence had also used his earnings and Social Security disability benefits to make some mortgage payments. Hicks had contributed towards the loan as well, but her payments were not consistent throughout the period.The court also considered the fact that Hicks had lived in the house for several years. It found that she had received value from the money she spent because she had been able to use the property as her home during that time.Her demand for compensation for mortgage payments and improvements was therefore rejected.Hicks challenged the lower court's decision on several grounds, including her claim that she had not been given a proper opportunity to question Mack during the trial.However, the appeals court found that Hicks had not taken the required steps to bring Mack into the proceedings as a witness. She had neither included her in the list of witnesses nor taken steps to secure her appearance.The court also noted that Hicks had not raised an objection during the trial. It therefore rejected her argument that she had been denied an opportunity to question Mack.The appeals court further found that Hicks had not provided enough material to show that the lower court had made an error while deciding the case.It ultimately upheld the earlier judgment, confirming Mack's ownership of the Phoenix house and rejecting Hicks's claims for ownership and compensation.
Article Summary: Court rules estranged wife owns Phoenix home, rejects partner's 24-year claim. Dimica Hicks moved into the property with Troy Torrence in 2000. She continued to live there until his death in September 2024. After his death, Hicks was appointed to handle his estate and approached the court seeking rights over the house. She argued that her long stay at the property and financial contributions towards it gave her a claim to ownership.

Article Title: An Illinois nursing assistant was allegedly asked to take unpaid leave for the rest of her pregnancy because she could not lift heavy weights at work; her employer will now pay $160,000 after she file
Article Text:
Representative image generated using AI

The pregnant employee couldn’t lift weights, so they fired her

Lifting was essential or go home without pay

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A pregnancy discrimination lawsuit

Prairie Green at Fay's Point, an assisted living facility in Blue Island, Illinois, will pay $160,000 in lost wages to a former nursing assistant under a federal settlement, the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) announced in a press release on 17 November. The EEOC sued the facility in September 2025 after the company fired a pregnant woman who had developed a pregnancy-related lifting restriction.According to the pregnancy discrimination lawsuit filed by the EEOC, the facility violated the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA) when it terminated a certified nursing assistant after she developed a pregnancy-related lifting restriction. The company allegedly told her that lifting weights was an essential part of her job and gave her only one option: to take unpaid leave for the rest of her pregnancy.Arinnie Young started working at the facility in December 2020 as a certified nursing assistant, according to a Chicago Tribune report. In April 2023, she told the director of nursing that she was pregnant. She also gave the company a doctor's note stating that she could not lift more than 20 pounds or lift residents, according to the EEOC's complaint. For a while, Young avoided lifting residents by swapping them with a co-worker, without making a formal accommodation request, the complaint says.Young made an official request, but it was denied. Officials told her that unpaid leave for the rest of her pregnancy was her only option, the EEOC said. She refused, and the company dismissed her on 15 August 2023. This conduct violated the PWFA, which requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations for pregnancy-related restrictions unless doing so would cause an undue hardship for the business. These accommodations may include temporarily excusing an employee from an essential job duty, modifying her responsibilities, offering light-duty work or assigning her to a vacant position. The law also prohibits employers from forcing pregnant employees to take leave when other reasonable accommodations would allow them to continue working.“The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act requires employers to consider reasonable accommodations that allow pregnant employees to remain on the job, including temporary modifications to their duties or reassignment to a vacant position,” EEOC Chair Andrea R. Lucas said.The EEOC also alleged that the facility advertised a concierge position less than a month later, but management never told Young about the opening or offered it to her. She could have performed that work despite her lifting restriction, the agency said.The EEOC first attempted to resolve the matter through its administrative conciliation process, but the effort failed. The agency then filed a lawsuit in the US District Court for the Northern District of Illinois under the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, a federal law that requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations for pregnancy-related restrictions unless doing so would cause an undue hardship.The company must pay Young $160,000 in lost wages. With this settlement, the case ends without a trial. It must also review and revise its pregnancy accommodation policies and establish guidelines for accommodations in jobs that require lifting. Employees will receive annual training on their rights and the employer's obligations under the law.Lucas said the agency would hold employers accountable. “Employers cannot simply force pregnant workers onto unpaid leave when reasonable accommodations are available. This settlement sends a clear message that the EEOC will hold employers accountable for failing to meet their obligations under the PWFA.”
Article Summary: Prairie Green at Fay's Point, an assisted living facility in Blue Island, Illinois, will pay $160,000 in lost wages to a former nursing assistant. The company allegedly told her that lifting weights was an essential part of her job and gave her only one option: to take unpaid leave for the rest of her pregnancy. The EEOC sued the facility in September 2025 after the company fired a pregnant woman who had developed a pregnancy-related lifting restriction.

Article Title: Minnesota couple found guilty of $15 million healthcare fraud after billing insurers for fake treatments and unlicensed care, then spending proceeds on luxury cars and a mansion
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How the couple carried out the $15 million Medicare fraud scheme

Couple established neurofeedback company to target elderly patients

Couple disguised neurofeedback treatments to bill Medicare

Couple spent $15 million in fraudulent Medicare payments on a lavish lifestyle

Auditor found only 9 per cent of the company's medical bills were supported

How the $15 million Medicare fraud scheme unravelled and led to guilty verdicts

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A Minnesota couple has been found guilty of defrauding Medicare, Medicaid and private health insurers of more than $15 million through a medical billing scam that targeted elderly and vulnerable patients. Gabriel Adam Alexander Luthor, 40, and Elizabeth Christine Brown, 43, used their neurofeedback therapy company, Golden Victory Medical, to submit false claims for treatments that were never provided, services carried out by unlicensed technicians and appointments that were recorded as lasting longer than they did. A federal jury found both defendants guilty of six counts of wire fraud and one count of money laundering following an 11-day trial.According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Luthor and Brown used their neurofeedback therapy company, Golden Victory Medical (GVM), to submit false medical bills to Medicare, Medicaid and other health insurers.The company billed for medical services that never took place, services performed by unlicensed technicians under the names of licensed professionals, and appointments falsely recorded as lasting longer than they actually did.On 586 days, GVM claimed in its insurance bills that its providers had spent more than 24 hours with patients.The scheme began in 2018, when Luthor and Brown, who were in a romantic relationship, lived in Las Vegas, Nevada. Brown held a master's degree in nursing and was licensed as an advanced practice registered nurse, commonly known as a nurse practitioner. Luthor had no medical training.In April 2018, Brown established GVM, and Luthor became a co-owner shortly afterwards. The couple identified potential patients, many of whom were elderly, confined to their homes or receiving hospice care. They arranged home visits by unlicensed neurofeedback technicians three times a week for treatment sessions.Neurofeedback is an investigational or alternative medical service that is not covered by Medicare or virtually any private health insurer. To obtain insurance payments, Luthor and Brown billed for other services, including neurobehavioural and psychological examinations.However, according to the DOJ, the vast majority of these billed services never took place, could not legally be performed by unlicensed and unsupervised technicians, or involved claims that significantly overstated the time spent with patients.The couple also failed to charge GVM patients their required co-payments, in violation of Medicare requirements. The DOJ said this meant many of the company's largely elderly patients did not notice or challenge the substantial amounts being billed to their insurance policies, although some patients raised complaints.Through the scheme, Luthor and Brown obtained more than $15 million from health insurers. The DOJ said they used the proceeds to substantially increase their standard of living, purchasing luxury vehicles and a mansion in Eden Prairie, Minnesota.In 2019, the couple moved from Las Vegas to Minnesota and bought a million-dollar mansion measuring 9,000 square feet. The property was purchased using proceeds from the fraud, and they relocated GVM's operational headquarters to the house.The couple also spent large sums on luxury travel to destinations including Vail and Miami, as well as regular visits to nightclubs where their bar bills exceeded $10,000, according to the DOJ.Luthor and Brown were repeatedly warned about their billing practices, but continued submitting false claims. A doctor who worked with Brown complained about her billing to the nursing boards in Nevada and Minnesota. A nurse practitioner also resigned and reported that GVM was submitting bills under her name for services she had not provided.A retired journalist separately complained that the company had billed insurers for medical services she had never received. The Centres for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) subsequently suspended Medicare payments to GVM over suspected fraud.An independent auditor found that only 9 per cent of GVM's billing codes were supported. The company's chief executive also warned Luthor and Brown that the billing problems could lead to serious legal consequences if they were not corrected. The couple fired the executive in retaliation, according to the DOJ. They also dismissed an outside billing contractor who warned them that the company was charging insurers too much for the services performed.The DOJ said Luthor and Brown also laundered proceeds from their fraudulent activities by transferring approximately $350,000 through a series of bank accounts. The money was used to fund an investment in water-well drilling in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.In early 2023, law enforcement officers executed search warrants at the couple's Eden Prairie residence and GVM's clinic in Las Vegas. The company subsequently ceased operations.Luthor and Brown were each convicted of six counts of wire fraud and one count of money laundering. Wire fraud carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years, while money laundering carries a maximum sentence of 10 years.Announcing the verdict, US Attorney Daniel N. Rosen said: “The defendants took advantage of elderly patients and viewed them like an ATM, thinking they could just punch in the right codes, and money would come pouring out.”Rosen also commended the law enforcement agencies involved in the investigation, adding that his office would continue to pursue fraud cases. The investigation involved the US Postal Inspection Service, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Eden Prairie Police Department, the US Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General and the US Marshals Service.
Article Summary: Gabriel Adam Alexander Luthor, 40, and Elizabeth Christine Brown, 43, used their neurofeedback therapy company, Golden Victory Medical, to submit false claims to Medicare, Medicaid and other health insurers. The company billed for medical services that never took place, services performed by unlicensed technicians under the names of licensed professionals, and appointments falsely recorded as lasting longer than they actually did. A federal jury found both defendants guilty of six counts of wire fraud and one count of money laundering following an 11-day trial.

Article Title: JeM commander acknowledges terror network in Rawalakot
Article Text:
With the Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed increasingly coming under scrutiny for operating proxy terror outfits in Jammu and Kashmir, their focus has shifted towards reviving dormant militant groups in the Valley and using them to further their activities.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In a significant admission exposing the nexus between terror outfits and Pakistani establishment, Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) commander Masood Ilyas Kashmiri has publicly acknowledged the presence of his group’s armed terrorist network in Rawalakot in POK while alleging state authorities plan to target leaders of an ongoing regional protest movement.Addressing a gathering in Islamabad, Ilyas also criticised Pakistan’s security and intelligence agencies, questioning their failure to identify individuals allegedly involved in anti-state activities as well as those accused of killing paramilitary Pakistan Rangers personnel during recent clashes.The JeM commander went on to say that some of his group’s armed cadres belong to the same local communities that are participating in demonstrations being organised by Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a civil society coalition that has led prolonged protests over economic grievances and governance in the region.He said he had also met with Pakistani govt and security officials in Islamabad to clarify JeM’s position on the unrest. During his address, he alleged officials in Pakistan’s leadership had decided to eliminate both the leaders of the action committee and chief demonstrators in Rawalakot.Ilyas previously drew attention in Sept 2025 when he was seen in a video addressing a gathering in Balakot and acknowledging significant losses suffered by JeM during Indian military strikes on May 7 that year under Operation Sindoor.More than 150 people have died in the protests against Pakistani govt in Rawalakot in the last few months. Ilyas’s statement has brought govt’s role in the open.Amid turmoil and rising casualties of peaceful protesters in Rawalkot and neighbouring regions of POK, JAAC had recently written to Field Marshal Asim Munir, demanding an immediate end to military operations.The committee had emphasised that continued state violence will only widen the rift between the Pakistani military establishment and the local population, risking the transformation of a peaceful and democratic movement into a violent uprising.
Article Summary: Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) commander Masood Ilyas Kashmiri has publicly acknowledged the presence of his group’s armed terrorist network in Rawalakot in POK. Article Title: Why thousands are protesting in Karachi against Asim Munir's proposal to divide Sindh
Article Text:
Sindhi nationalist groups rally in Karachi, opposing alleged plans to divide Sindh and accusing Asim Munir of undermining the province's unity (Image credit: Ayaz Latif Palijo's X)

Why Sindhi nationalist groups are opposing proposed division

Resource exploitation, land takeover allegations

JSMM announces economic blockade, Sindhudesh campaign

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Thousands of people, including political leaders and activists from various Sindhi nationalist organisations, rallied in Karachi on Monday to oppose alleged moves to divide Sindh into new administrative units.The demonstration, organised by the Jeay Sindh Rahbar Committee, accused Pakistan's Army Chief Asim Munir and Punjab of attempting to weaken Sindh's territorial unity, while raising concerns over alleged economic exploitation and control of the province's resources.The rally brought together several nationalist groups from different parts of Sindh, with opposition to the proposed administrative changes emerging as the central theme of the demonstration.According to a press release issued by the organisers, the rally was led by prominent nationalist leaders, including Riaz Chandio, Dr Niaz Kalani, Aslam Khairpuri and Nawaz Khan Zaunr, along with other senior political figures, ANI reported.Organisations participating in the demonstration included Jeay Sindh Qaumi Mahaz (Bashir Khan), Jeay Sindh Qaumi Mahaz (Aresar), Jeay Sindh Qaumparast Party and Jeay Sindh Qaumi Mahaz (Niaz Kalani).Activists of Jeay Sindh Muttahida Mahaz (JSMM), which is not formally part of the Jeay Sindh Rahbar Committee, also joined the rally.The organisers accused Punjab and Pakistan's army Chief Asim Munir of pursuing attempts to weaken Sindh's historical, territorial and national unity through the creation of new administrative units. They alleged that the proposed changes were a pretext to fragment the province.Participants declared that they would not accept any division of Sindh and insisted that its historical and geographical unity must be protected.The organisers described Pakistan as an artificial theocratic state and alleged that Sindh had faced political subordination and economic exploitation since its incorporation into the country. They asserted that the Sindhi nation had historically existed as an ancient and sovereign community.The rally also highlighted allegations of exploitation of Sindh's natural resources and agricultural land. According to the organisers, millions of acres of ancestral agricultural land, coastal islands and reserves of oil, natural gas and coal had been taken over by Punjab and the Pakistani state apparatus.The demonstration was organised to register opposition to what the groups described as internal colonial control of Sindh and to mobilise support against any proposed administrative division of the province.In a separate announcement, the central body of Jeay Sindh Muttahida Mahaz (JSMM) said it would intensify its political struggle by launching an economic blockade targeting Punjab.According to the press release, the decision was taken during a meeting of the organisation's central leadership a day before the Karachi rally. JSMM announced plans to enforce a shutdown of highways and transit routes to disrupt supply lines to Punjab.The organisation also said its movement, initially focused on defending Sindh's territorial integrity, would be expanded into a campaign demanding the complete national independence of Sindhudesh.The press release said JSMM planned to mobilise the Sindhi population, particularly young people, for sustained political mobilisation and resistance towards achieving independence from what it described as Punjabi colonial occupation.
Article Summary: Sindhi nationalist groups rally in Karachi, opposing alleged plans to divide Sindh. Accuse Pakistan's Army Chief Asim Munir of undermining the province's unity. Thousands of people, including political leaders and activists from various Sindhi nationalist organisations, rally.

Article Title: LeT, JeM proxies exposed, ISI eyes revival of 19 dormant terror outfits in Jammu and Kashmir
Article Text:
How ISI plans to rebuild terror networks in J&K

19 dormant terror outfits on ISI radar

Local recruitment, infiltration among key concerns

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence ( ISI ) is exploring a shift in its strategy in Jammu and Kashmir , with plans to bring back dormant terror outfits in the Valley as its existing proxy groups face increased scrutiny from the security agencies, news agency IANS reported.Pakistan's ugly motive is to create a network of revived terror outfits that can operate without any apparent links to established Pakistan-based organisations such as the Lashkar-e-Taiba ( LeT ) and Jaish-e-Mohammed ( JeM ), according to officials cited by IANS.The Hafiz Saeed-led LeT has been operating through The Resistance Front (TRF), while Masood Azhar's JeM has been linked to proxy outfits such as the People's Anti-Fascist Front (PAFF), Kashmir Tigers (KT) and Lashkar-e-Mustafa.However, investigations by agencies such as the Jammu and Kashmir Police and the National Investigation Agency (NIA) have increasingly exposed the links between these outfits and their parent organisations. The agencies have gathered evidence indicating that the different names are being used to mask the involvement of the LeT and JeM.An official told IANS that the ISI has now advised these groups to reconnect with former members of terror organisations that have been inactive in Jammu and Kashmir for years.Several of these outfits emerged during the 1990s and early 2000s, when militancy was at its peak in the Valley. However, as the ISI concentrated its operations around the LeT, JeM and Hizbul Mujahideen, many smaller groups gradually became inactive.Some ran out of funds, while others lost their operatives to security force operations, the official said.According to data cited by IANS, Jammu and Kashmir currently has 10 active terror groups, while 19 outfits remain inactive. Among the dormant organisations are the Kashmir Jehad Force (KJF) and Tehrik-e-Jihad (TeJ).An Intelligence Bureau official said the ISI is likely to focus on locating former members of these groups and encouraging them to rebuild their networks."These members would be told to look out for potential recruits and then revive these terror groups. There would be no direct link between these groups and the existing terror outfits. This helps the ISI in covering its tracks when an investigation into a terror attack is launched," the official said.A major consideration behind the proposed strategy is that several of these organisations are homegrown rather than Pakistan-based. Their revival could make it more difficult for investigators to establish direct links with established terror outfits operating from across the border, the report said.The ISI is also expected to draw on the experience of former members in areas such as recruitment and logistics. Although many of them are now older, officials believe their knowledge of local networks could prove useful in rebuilding the outfits.The agency is likely to focus on recruiting local youth, while Pakistan continues to explore ways to increase infiltration into Jammu and Kashmir through multiple routes, an official told IANS.Another official said the ISI is keen to restore militant activity in the Valley. However, the recent killing of Lashkar commander Lateef Bhat has dealt a setback to its plans and could delay efforts to revive terror networks for some time.The revived groups could be used for both ground operations and information warfare, including disinformation and propaganda campaigns, officials said.This would require security agencies to tackle not only possible terror operations but also coordinated attempts to influence public opinion through propaganda, adding to the security challenges in Jammu and Kashmir, the report said.
Article Summary: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence ( ISI ) is exploring a shift in its strategy in Jammu and Kashmir. It plans to bring back dormant terror outfits in the Valley as its existing proxy groups face increased scrutiny. The revived groups could be used for both ground operations and information warfare, including disinformation and propaganda campaigns.

Article Title: Pakistan petrol pumps threaten nationwide shutdown, give govt 15 days to meet demands
Article Text:
Pakistan's fuel crisis fears grow as petrol dealers threaten nationwide shutdown

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan's petroleum dealers have threatened to shut down petrol pumps across the country if the government fails to introduce a monthly fuel pricing mechanism, giving authorities 15 days to address their demands, according to a report by Dawn.The Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) said frequent revisions in petroleum prices were causing serious financial difficulties for fuel retailers and rapidly depleting their working capital. The association warned that continued uncertainty could force petrol pumps to suspend operations, potentially triggering a law and order situation.Addressing a presser at the Karachi Press Club, PPDA chairman Malik Khuda Bakhsh, along with other association representatives, demanded that dealers' profit margins be raised to 8 per cent of the retail price. They also alleged that refineries had cut petrol and diesel supplies, with one refinery reportedly halting diesel supplies altogether, Dawn reported.The dealers claimed that they collectively contribute PKR 5.74 billion to the national exchequer every day and urged the government to take their financial concerns into account before introducing further changes to petroleum-related policies.Khuda Bakhsh said previous strike threats had been withdrawn following government intervention, but several demands remained unresolved.He argued that changing market conditions following the US-Iran war made it necessary for the authorities to reconsider the existing pricing arrangement, according to Dawn.Pakistan introduced the daily fuel pricing mechanism in July, citing volatility in international oil markets. Under the system, the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA) announces revised petroleum prices every day.The PPDA has repeatedly opposed the arrangement, demanding a return to monthly or fortnightly price revisions. Earlier, another petroleum dealers' association had also postponed its nationwide strike following assurances from the petroleum minister that the daily pricing system would initially operate on a trial basis.In August, the government approved a 15.5 per cent increase in dealers' margins on petrol and high-speed diesel. The move raised the margin by PKR 1.34 per litre to PKR 9.98, effective September 1. However, the dealers' demand for an 8 per cent margin remains unresolved.
Article Summary: Pakistan's petroleum dealers have threatened to shut down petrol pumps across the country if the government fails to introduce a monthly fuel pricing mechanism. The Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association said frequent revisions in petroleum prices were causing serious financial difficulties for fuel retailers. The association warned that continued uncertainty could force petrol pumps to suspend operations.

Article Title: SCO: Pakistan set to invite India for culture ministers' meeting
Article Text:
The only significant visit to Pakistan from India after the April 2025 Pahalgam attack was by MEA additional secretary Alok Dimri for a meeting of the SCO national coordinators in September

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

After participating in the SCO inaugural civilisational dialogue in New Delhi, Pakistan is now all set to deliver an invitation to India for a meeting of the culture ministers it will host under its presidency of the Eurasian bloc early next year. It will be interesting to see how India responds as no Indian minister has visited Pakistan since the Pahalgam terrorist attack.Significantly, Islamabad is also preparing to host the SCO heads of state council summit - where India is usually represented by PM Narendra Modi -next year in late August, after initially considering having it on August 14 – Pakistan's Independence Day. An August 14 summit is unlikely to have seen participation by India at any level.The only significant visit to Pakistan from India after the April 2025 Pahalgam attack was by MEA additional secretary Alok Dimri for a meeting of the SCO national coordinators in September – shortly after Pakistan assumed presidency – to firm up the calendar of events under Islamabad's stewardship.After what is officially called Meeting of Ministers of Culture (SCO-MMC), Pakistan will also host more high-profile meetings of the SCO defence and foreign ministers in the run up to the Islamabad summit in August.The meeting for cultural cooperation among SCO member-states in Pakistan is a relatively low-stakes event for India that keeps political commitments minimal, unlike the foreign and defence high-level gatherings which might raise the political temperature at home.The last minister to visit Pakistan was S Jaishankar for a meeting of the SCO foreign ministers' meeting in October 2024, well before Pahalgam.Amid criticism by the Opposition for hosting Pakistan minister Musadik Malik for the Modi-proposed civilisational dialogue last week, India reiterated there was no dilution of its position on the Indus Waters Treaty that was "put in abeyance" after the Pahalgam attack. India has stressed that SCO cooperation should not be mistaken for bilateral thaw.The visit by Malik passed off smoothly without any bilateral friction as he adhered to the protocol of addressing multilateral SCO themes, rather than raising sensitive bilateral issues.While the key question remains whether Modi will travel to Islamabad for the SCO summit, Indian officials say such a visit is highly improbable at this stage. Any bilateral thaw that might result in Modi's visit requires, as far as India is concerned, a fundamental shift in Pakistan's position on cross-border terrorism.India is seeking tangible progress on its security concerns and doesn't want to create any optics of normalisation when these concerns remain unaddressed.The possibility of a senior minister, most likely Jaishankar, representing India is not ruled out. It would allow India to sustain its active engagement with the SCO, while not being seen as softening its Pakistan policy. Officials point to the fact that there's already a precedent for that. In 2024, it was Jaishankar who attended the heads of summit in Kazakhstan, filling in for the PM.
Article Summary: Pakistan is set to deliver an invitation to India for a meeting of the culture ministers it will host under its presidency of the Eurasian bloc early next year. No Indian minister has visited Pakistan since the Pahalgam terrorist attack. Islamabad is also preparing to host the SCO heads of state council summit next year in late August.

Article Title: Lahore tops global pollution ranking again as AQI crosses 500, eight Pakistan cities among worst
Article Text:
Choking under state neglect: Lahore once again ranks world’s most polluted city as AQI breaches 500

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Lahore once again ranked as the world's most polluted major city on Sunday morning, with its Air Quality Index (AQI) reaching 538, placing it in the hazardous category, according to Pakistani daily Dawn. Eight cities in Punjab also featured among Pakistan's 10 most polluted urban centres, as severe smog continued to affect the province.Data from Swiss air quality monitoring platform IQAir showed Lahore at the top of the global major city ranking with an AQI of 538 between 9 am and 10 am. The reading exposed residents to severe health risks associated with hazardous air pollution.Karachi was further down the global ranking with an AQI of 180, followed by Cairo at 162.The pollution crisis extended beyond Lahore, with Kahna Nau in Lahore district recording the worst air quality in Pakistan at an AQI of 606. It was followed by Lahore at 538, Bahawalpur at 536, Sargodha at 392 and Gujranwala at 347, Dawn reported.Multan, Dera Ghazi Khan, Skardu, Faisalabad and Peshawar completed the list of the country's 10 most polluted cities.Lahore has repeatedly featured at the top of global pollution rankings in recent weeks.It recorded an AQI of 266 on Saturday evening, while the city had logged an hourly reading of 465 between 7 am and 8 am on Friday, as heavy smog affected several parts of Punjab.The continuing pollution has raised questions over the effectiveness of the Punjab administration's anti-smog measures. Lahore Traffic Police, however, has claimed that enforcement against vehicles contributing to air pollution has been stepped up.Chief Traffic Officer Syed Abdul Rahim Shirazi said on Saturday that traffic personnel had issued challan tickets to 14,653 vehicles emitting smoke. Action was also taken against 10,306 vehicles transporting sand, soil and other materials without tarpaulin covers. Police penalised 31,618 unfit and dilapidated vehicles and took action against 272,760 overloaded vehicles, he added.Separately, enforcement squads from the Punjab Environment Protection and Climate Change Department conducted 84,370 inspections of brick kilns across the province between January 1 and November 18, Dawn reported earlier this week. During this period, authorities demolished 1,429 kilns, sealed 968 and registered 1,248 FIRs against violators.Between September 1 and November 18, which covers the peak smog period, the department carried out 29,999 inspections, demolished 519 kilns, sealed 494 and registered 408 FIRs. It also imposed fines worth PKR 101.45 million.The scale of Pakistan's air pollution is also reflected in long-term data. The 2025 World Air Quality Report put the country's average PM2.5 concentration at 67.3 micrograms per cubic metre, nearly 14 times the World Health Organisation's annual guideline of 5 micrograms per cubic metre, Dawn reported.The report also placed Pakistan among the world's most polluted countries, with an average AQI of 156.Globally, indoor and outdoor air pollution together account for an estimated 8.1 million deaths annually, making air pollution the second-leading risk factor for mortality worldwide. Outdoor particulate matter alone is responsible for an estimated 4.7 million deaths.
Article Summary: Lahore once again ranks world’s most polluted city as AQI breaches 500. Eight cities in Punjab also featured among Pakistan's 10 most polluted urban centres. Lahore Traffic Police claims enforcement against vehicles contributing to air pollution has been stepped up.

Article Title: 4.0-magnitude earthquake strikes Pakistan near Afghanistan border
Article Text:

Seven people were killed in a clash between two tribes over the ownership of a forest in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, news agency PTI reported, quoting police Saturday.The incident took place around 10pm local time on Thursday at Bilija forest in Battagram district, when armed members of the Gilal and Kaloch tribes confronted each other, leading to an exchange of gunfire.According to police, armed men from the Kaloch tribe took positions and opened fire, prompting retaliation from the Gilal side. Four members of the Gilal tribe and three from the Kaloch tribe were killed in the clash.The two tribes have been involved in a longstanding dispute over the ownership of Bilija forest, which has continued for several decades and claimed several lives in the past, police said.The Gilal tribe is associated with the Allai valley in Battagram district, while the Kaloch community belongs to neighbouring Kohistan district.Police said repeated efforts by the administrations of both districts to resolve the dispute and bring the communities together had failed to produce a permanent solution.The latest clash has once again raised concerns over the law and order situation in Imran Khan 's stronghold Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Article Title: 'I call for Imran Khan's release': UN rights chief flags ex-Pakistan PM's health, jail conditions
Article Text:
UN steps up pressure on Pakistan over Imran Khan's detention

Amnesty raises concerns over Khan's health

Family members' detention draws scrutiny
